passages.title: Be mindful of Allah, not of the disbelievers
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Surah al-Ahzab opens with Allah speaking directly to His Messenger ﷺ and giving him one instruction in four movements: be conscious of Allah, pay no heed to the disbelievers and the hypocrites (ayah 1), take your direction from revelation alone (ayah 2), and lean your whole weight on Allah (ayah 3). Behind the passage lie several reported episodes in which the Prophet ﷺ was pressed — by inducement, by threat, and by requests for a small concession. The answer given is not a debating point. It is a re-ordering of where he places his fear, his listening, his guidance and his reliance.

## The surah these ayat open

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that al-Ahzab is a Madani surah, and that most of its subject matter concerns the beloved person of the Holy Prophet ﷺ and his special place with Allah. It repeatedly stresses that showing reverence to him is obligatory and that causing him any pain is haram (forbidden), and the surah's other themes serve as complements to the perfection of his station. Read that way, an opening that addresses him personally — "O Prophet" — is not incidental. It sets the key the whole surah is sung in.

## Why these ayat came down

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers three reports about the occasion of revelation.

**One — the neighbours who came as friends.** When the Prophet ﷺ settled in Madinah after the hijrah, the areas around the city were inhabited by Jewish tribes, among them Qurayzah, Nadir and Banu Qaynuqaʿ. Being a prophet of mercy for all, he wished and worked for them to embrace Islam. Some men among them began visiting him and posing as Muslims hypocritically, with no faith in their hearts. He treated this as a beginning worth building on — hoping that if some accepted Islam it would become easier to invite the rest — so he welcomed these men particularly warmly, and even when they did something bad he would overlook it as a matter of religious expediency. It was on account of this that the opening ayat of al-Ahzab were revealed. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qurtubi.)

**Two — the bribe and the threat.** Reported by Ibn Jarir from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas: after the hijrah, Walid ibn Mughirah and Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, from among the disbelievers of Makkah, came to Madinah and offered the Prophet ﷺ half of the entire wealth of the Quraysh of Makkah if he would withdraw his claim to prophethood. And the hypocrites and Jews of Madinah threatened to kill him if he did not withdraw from his claim and his call. Thereupon these ayat were revealed. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ruh al-Maʿani.)

**Three — the request for a half-step.** Reported by Thaʿalibi and Wahidi *with no ascription of authority.* This one goes back to the time after a no-war pact was signed at Hudaybiyah between the pagans of Makkah and the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Sufyan, ʿIkrimah, Ibn Abi Jahl and Abu al-Aʿwar al-Sulami came to Madinah and said to him: stop speaking ill of our objects of worship — or simply say that they too will intercede on our behalf and bring us benefits; if you do just that much, we for our part will forget about you and your Lord, and the dispute will be all over. What they said was very unpleasant for the Prophet ﷺ and for the Muslims, who wanted to kill them. He said: "I have made a peace pact with them, therefore, this cannot be done." Thereupon these ayat were revealed. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ruh al-Maʿani.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that although the reports differ, there is in reality no contradiction between them; these events could together be the cause of the revelation of these ayat. And notice how they map onto the two commands of ayah 1: **fear Allah**, because killing men under a treaty was a breach of trust, which is haram; and **do not obey the disbelievers**, because the demands made by them in all these events were unacceptable.

## "O Prophet" — the address itself

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the wording. Nowhere in the entire Qur'an is the final Messenger ﷺ addressed directly by his personal name, in the way other prophets are: *O Adam, O Nuh, O Ibrahim, O Musa*, repeatedly. He is always addressed by a title — *nabiyy* (prophet) or *rasul* (messenger). The only exceptions are four places where his blessed name appears [3:144; 33:40; 47:2; 48:29], and there the very purpose was to declare that he is the Messenger of Allah, so naming him was functionally necessary. That is a singular honour and a mark of the high regard in which he is held. The surah begins by honouring him — and only then commands him.

## Taqwa: what is actually being asked

Ibn Kathir cites Talq bin Habib's definition, worth carrying around: **"Taqwa means obeying Allah in the light of the guidance of Allah and in hope of earning the reward of Allah, and refraining from disobeying Allah in the light of the guidance of Allah and fearing the punishment of Allah."**

Two things stand out. Taqwa is not a vague nervousness; it has content — obedience and abstention, both *in the light of guidance*, not in the light of one's own instincts. And it runs on two rails: hope of reward and fear of punishment.

Here taqwa also has a sharp, concrete edge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "fear Allah" was placed first precisely because the Muslims wanted to kill the Makkan idolaters with whom a treaty of peace was already in effect; the instruction to avoid a breach of pledge therefore had to come first. As for yielding to the disbelievers, since no one had even wanted to do that, it was mentioned later. The order of the two commands is the order of the actual danger.

## Why command a Prophet who cannot sin?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: the Prophet ﷺ was maʿsum — protected, in the sense that there was simply no probability of divine injunctions being contravened by him. Breaking a solemn pledge is a major sin; accepting the offer of the disbelievers and polytheists would likewise be a grave sin. Why command him at all?

Two answers are given. **Ruh al-Maʿani**: these orders carry the sense of an instruction to abide by this conduct in the future as well, just as he had done in the incident itself. **Some respected commentators**: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the purpose is to warn the Muslim community at large. The law is for the whole community, so a corresponding mode was employed to make the community hear it and become alert — and addressing the Prophet ﷺ enhanced the importance of the order significantly, suggesting: when even the Messenger of Allah is the addressee of the order, how can any individual Muslim consider himself exempt?

Ibn Kathir states the same principle as a rule of Qur'anic style: **"Here Allah points out something lower by referring to something higher. When He commands His servant and Messenger to do this, He is also commanding those who are lower than him, and the command is addressed to them more so."** Whenever you read a command given to the Prophet ﷺ, read yourself into it — with more urgency, not less.

## "Do not obey them" means: do not let them into the room

Ibn Kathir's gloss on *wa lā tuṭiʿi l-kāfirīna wa l-munāfiqīn* is strikingly practical: **"means, do not listen to what they say and do not consult them."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds this. Ibn Kathir's point, it says, is that the real purpose of forbidding obedience to the disbelievers here is that the Prophet ﷺ should not consult with them or let them have the opportunity of sitting with him frequently — because such consultation or mutual interaction generally becomes the cause of ending up in a disposition favouring the acceptance of what they proposed. There was no probability whatsoever that he would do what they asked. Even so, he was stopped from maintaining such liaison with them and from having them participate in his consultations. This is the idea expressed by the word *iṭāʿah* — obedience, submission, or listening to and doing the bidding of someone. What has really been done, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is that he has been prohibited from adopting the ways that could lead to such obedience. As for obedience itself, there was never any probability of it.

This is why the first reported occasion — the warm welcome extended to insincere visitors — is not a small matter. The danger was never that the Prophet ﷺ would be argued out of Islam. It was that a policy of extra civility and accommodation toward people with no faith in their hearts would quietly set the terms of the conversation.

## Why the hypocrites are named separately

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān poses another question: the ayah implies that both disbelievers and hypocrites were proposing things counter to the true Islamic position. From open disbelievers that is expected. But if a hypocrite said something openly against Islam he would no longer be a hypocrite — he would be an open disbeliever. So why mention them separately?

The answer offered: it is possible that the hypocrites did not say anything against Islam very openly, but said something in support of the other disbelievers. And if the incident of the Jewish visitors is taken as the occasion of revelation, the difficulty disappears entirely — because on that reading the Prophet ﷺ is simply being prohibited from dealing with Jews who called themselves Muslims in a spirit of extra civility and accommodation.

## "Verily, Allah is Ever All-Knower, All-Wise"

Ayah 1 closes by grounding the command in who Allah is. Ibn Kathir: this **"means, He is more deserving of your following His commandments and obeying Him, for He knows the consequences of all things and is Wise in all that He says and does."** The logic is a comparison. Two parties are offering direction: people who see one move ahead, and the One who knows how everything ends.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the situational point. The proposals put forward by the disbelievers and hypocrites did promise certain real-looking advantages — lesser tension, increased mutual tolerance. But Allah, who knows the consequences of everything, is most wise and fully aware of what is better for His servants, and He prohibited this by declaring that even that degree of tolerance was counter to what was expedient under the circumstances, and that such a policy was not going to end well.

## Ayah 2: refusal is only half of it

*And follow that which is revealed to you from your Lord.* Ibn Kathir explains "that which is revealed" as **the Qur'an and Sunnah**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this ayah the complement of the first order: do not be beguiled or taken in by what the disbelievers and hypocrites say, and do not agree or yield to it — and instead of all that, whatever Allah has told you through waḥy (revelation) remains the only thing you and your companions should follow. Rejection alone leaves a vacuum; this ayah fills it. A person who merely refuses his opponents' advice is still being steered by them, in reverse. A person following revelation is being steered by Allah.

Then comes a shift in the Arabic. The ayah begins in the singular — *follow*, addressed to him alone — and ends in the plural: *bimā taʿmalūn*, "with what **you all** do." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that since the noble Companions and the Muslims at large are included under this address, by putting "what you do" in the plural form at the end, everyone was alerted. The circle widens inside a single ayah.

The ayah closes: **"Verily, Allah is Well-Acquainted with what you do."** Ibn Kathir: **"nothing at all is hidden from Him."** Against opponents who trade in private offers and concealed motives, the community is reminded that the One they answer to misses nothing.

## Ayah 3: and lean on Him

*And put your trust in Allah, and sufficient is Allah as a Wakīl.* The two commentaries render *wakīl* as "Trustee" (Ibn Kathir) and "guardian" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

Ibn Kathir: put your trust in Allah **"in all your affairs and situations"**; and **"sufficient is He as a Trustee for the one who puts his trust in Him and turns to Him."** Read that last clause carefully — the sufficiency is described in relation to the person who actually entrusts his affairs to Allah and turns to Him. The guarantee is real, and it is attached to an act of the heart, not merely to a claim.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the force of this in context: as for your approach, just pay no heed to what they say; and in order to succeed in your objective, trust no one but Allah, for He in Himself and by Himself is the ultimate doer, maker and fixer of all matters and things — and with Him there, you do not need to acquiesce in the opinion of anyone. That is the engine of the whole passage. A person refuses a bribe and a death threat only when he genuinely believes his outcome is not in the hands of the people making them.

## A ruling drawn from these ayat

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: these ayat prove that **in religious matters, even consulting with disbelievers is not permissible. In other matters relating to technical or functional experience, there is no harm in doing so. And Allah knows best.**

The distinction is worth holding precisely. This is not a rule about avoiding people, trade, neighbourliness or expertise; a specialist is consulted for what he knows. But the question *what does Allah want of me* is not put to someone who does not accept that Allah has spoken.

## Living it

- **Keep your covenants, even with enemies** (ayah 1). The Prophet ﷺ refused to let the Muslims kill men he had a peace pact with, and Allah's first word to him in this surah was taqwa. Anger at genuine wrongdoing does not release a believer from an obligation he has taken on.
- **Choose carefully whose voice sits in your counsel** (ayah 1) — not because you fear losing an argument, but because, as Ibn Kathir explains it, frequent consultation and interaction of that kind generally end up producing a disposition favourable to what such people propose. The road was blocked, not just the destination.
- **Fill the space with revelation** (ayah 2) — the Qur'an and Sunnah — and remember that it is *you all* whose deeds Allah is Well-Acquainted with, not only the one being addressed.
- **Then put the outcome down** (ayah 3). Sufficient is Allah as a Trustee for the one who puts his trust in Him and turns to Him.

passages.title: Abolishing zihar, adoption, and false kinship
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat demolish a set of fictions the Arabs of Jahiliyyah lived by, and then name the two bonds that are real: the bond of faith to the Prophet ﷺ, and the bond of blood.

One principle holds the passage together: **words spoken by the mouth do not create realities.** Ayah 4 states it, ayah 5 applies it to names and lineage, and ayah 6 shows where true loyalty and true inheritance actually lie.

## The three customs being corrected

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names three notions current among the disbelievers:

1. That an unusually clever man had **two hearts in his chest**.
2. **Zihar** — a husband declaring his wife to be like the back of his mother: "You are, for me, like the back of my mother." The word comes from *zahr*, "back". They held that once a man said this, his wife became forbidden to him forever.
3. **Adoption** (*mutabannā*) — taking another man's son, calling him your own, and recognising him *in all rules and regulations* as a real son: he shared in inheritance alongside the children from the man's own loins, and his divorced wife was taken to be permanently forbidden to the adoptive father.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes why Allah begins with the two hearts. That notion was not tied up with religious belief or conduct, and its falsity was obvious to everyone; most likely it was introduced as a **prologue** to the other two: as plainly false as "two hearts in one chest" is, that is how false their notions about zihar and adopted sons are. Ibn Kathir reads the sequence the same way: before Allah discusses ideas and theoretical matters, He gives tangible examples — one man cannot have two hearts in his body; a wife does not become a mother by the words of zihar; and by the same token an adopted child does not become the son of the man who adopts him.

## An incident in the prayer rows

Ibn Kathir records, through Imam Ahmad, that Qabus's father asked Ibn ʿAbbas what the ayah about two hearts meant. Ibn ʿAbbas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up one day to pray, and he trembled. The hypocrites who were praying with him said, "Do you not see that he has two hearts, one heart with you and another with them?" Then Allah revealed the words, *"Allah has not made for any man two hearts inside his body."* This was also narrated by At-Tirmidhi, who said, "It is a Hasan Hadith" — *hasan* meaning sound. It was also narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, from the hadith of Zuhayr.

No chest holds two hearts, and no heart holds two loyalties.

## Zihar: the words that changed nothing

Allah says the wives you declare to be like your mothers' backs are *not* your mothers. Ibn Kathir pairs this with Sūrat al-Mujādilah: *"They cannot be their mothers. None can be their mothers except those who gave them birth"* (58:2). Motherhood is a fact of birth, not a fact of speech.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this demolishes the Jahili belief that zihar makes a wife forbidden **forever** — your mother is but she who gave birth to you. The standing injunction appears in Sūrat al-Mujādilah (58:2–4): the statement is called a sin, abstaining from it is obligatory, and a man who has made such a declaration must offer a *kaffārah* (expiation) for zihar, after which intimacy with his wife again becomes lawful for him. The words are not magic — but neither are they free.

## Adoption: the case of Zayd bin Harithah

Ibn Kathir states that *"nor has He made your adopted sons your real sons"* was revealed concerning **Zayd bin Harithah**, may Allah be pleased with him, the freed servant of the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ had adopted him **before prophethood**, and he was known as *Zayd bin Muhammad*. Allah wanted to put an end to this naming and attribution.

The Arabic for these adopted sons is *adʿiyāʾ*, plural of *daʿiyy*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses as a "so-called" son. The word itself concedes the point: he is a son by claim, not by origin. And so, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, he is neither entitled to a share in inheritance alongside the real sons, nor do the rules of unlawfulness in marriage apply to him.

Then: *dhālikum qawlukum bi-afwāhikum* — **"That is but your saying with your mouths."** Ibn Kathir explains: your adoption of him is just words, and it does not mean that he is really your son, for he was created from the loins of another man. And he ties the knot back to the opening image — **a child cannot have two fathers, just as a man cannot have two hearts in one body.**

Against this stands *"But Allah says the truth, and He guides to the way."* Saʿid bin Jubayr said "Allah says the truth" means **justice**; Qatadah said "and He guides to the way" means **the straight path**. Human speech invents; divine speech states what is, and then shows the road. Ibn Kathir connects this to the later declaration in the same sūrah: *"Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the last of the Prophets"* (33:40).

## Ayah 5: give the children back their names

*"Call them by their fathers — that is more just with Allah."* Ibn Kathir explains that this command **abrogates** the state of affairs that existed at the beginning of Islam, when it was permitted to call adopted sons after the man who adopted them.

Al-Bukhari narrated that ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar said that Zayd bin Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him, was always called Zayd bin Muhammad until this ayah was revealed; this was also narrated by Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i.

**What actually changed.** Ibn Kathir notes that they used to deal with adopted sons as sons in every respect, including being alone with them as maḥrams (unmarriageable relatives). Hence Sahlah bint Suhayl, the wife of Abu Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "O Messenger of Allah! We used to call Salim our son, but Allah has revealed what He has revealed. He used to enter upon me, but I feel that Abu Hudhayfah does not like that." The Prophet ﷺ said, *"Breastfeed him and he will become your Mahram."* For a foster son through breastfeeding is the same as a son born from one's own loins, because the Prophet ﷺ said, in the words recorded in the Two Sahihs, *"Suckling makes unlawful as lineage does."*

Because an adopted son is not a real son, the woman he divorces is not a son's wife — and Ibn Kathir points out that the prohibition in Sūrat an-Nisa' is worded precisely: *"The wives of your sons **from your own loins**"* (4:23). So Allah made it permissible for a man to marry the former wife of his adopted son, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married Zaynab bint Jahsh, the divorced wife of Zayd bin Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him — *"so that there may be no difficulty to the believers in respect of the wives of their adopted sons when the latter have no desire to keep them"* (33:37). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the human cost of the old fiction: this very matter threw the Quraysh of Arabia into deception and led them into a sin of terribly serious proportions, blaming the Prophet ﷺ for marrying the divorced wife of his "son". Much of this sūrah, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, concerns the pain inflicted on the Prophet ﷺ, and this accusation was among its sharpest forms.

## Is affectionate "my son" forbidden?

No. Ibn Kathir is explicit that calling a person "son" as an expression of honour and endearment is not what is forbidden here. He cites the report recorded by Imam Ahmad and the Sunan compilers — apart from At-Tirmidhi — from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the young boys of Banu ʿAbd al-Muttalib came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the Jamarat, and he said, *"O my sons, do not stone the Jamarah until the sun has risen."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a caution: calling another's child "son" out of simple affection, and not as a declaration of adoption, is permissible — yet it is not the better choice, because at least in appearance it looks like violating the prohibition (citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī from al-Khafājī ʿalā al-Bayḍāwī).

## When the father is not known

*"But if you know not their fathers, then they are your brothers in the religion and your mawālī (freed servants)."* Ibn Kathir explains that this compensates for not knowing what a person's real lineage is: he is to be called a brother in faith or a freed servant — a real bond, honestly named.

Ibn Kathir's illustration is the dispute over the daughter of Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with her. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ left Makkah after performing his ʿUmrat al-Qaḍāʾ, she started following him, calling, "O uncle, O uncle!" Then ʿAli, Zayd and Jaʿfar — may Allah be pleased with them — disputed over which of them would care for her. ʿAli said, "I have more right, because she is the daughter of my paternal uncle." Zayd said, "She is the daughter of my brother." Jaʿfar bin Abi Talib said, "She is the daughter of my paternal uncle and I am married to her maternal aunt" — meaning Asma' bint ʿUmays. The Prophet ﷺ ruled that she should stay with her maternal aunt, and said, *"The maternal aunt has the same status as the mother."*

Then he gave each man his due. To ʿAli: *"You belong to me and I belong to you."* To Jaʿfar: *"You resemble me both in your looks and in your attitude."* And to Zayd: *"You are our brother and our freed servant."* Ibn Kathir observes that the most important of the rulings in this hadith is that the Prophet ﷺ ruled according to the truth while also seeking to appease all the disputing parties — and that his words to Zayd are exactly what this ayah says. Zayd lost a borrowed surname and received a bond named by the Prophet ﷺ himself.

## Mistakes are forgiven; intentions are not

*"And there is no sin on you concerning that in which you made a mistake, except in regard to what your hearts deliberately intend."* Ibn Kathir explains: if you call one of them after someone who is not in fact his father, **by mistake**, after trying your best to find out his parentage, then Allah will not attach any sin to this mistake. He compares the du'a Allah commands His servants to say — *"Our Lord! Punish us not if we forget or fall into error"* (2:286) — and notes that it was reported in Sahih Muslim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said Allah has answered: *"Certainly I did (so)."*

He adds that in Sahih al-Bukhari it was recorded, on the authority of ʿAmr bin al-ʿAs, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"If the judge makes Ijtihad and reaches the right decision, he will have two rewards; if he makes Ijtihad and reaches the wrong decision, he will have one reward."* The sin, he says, falls on the person who **deliberately** does something wrong — as Allah says elsewhere, *"Allah will not call you to account for that which is unintentional in your oaths"* (2:225).

## Why lineage is treated so seriously

Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that ʿUmar said: "Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with the Truth and revealed to him the Book. One of the things that was revealed in it was the Ayah of stoning, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stoned [adulterers] and we stoned [them] after he died." Then ʿUmar said: "We also used to recite, 'Do not attribute yourselves to anyone other than your fathers, for this is disbelief, to attribute yourselves to anyone other than your fathers.'"

In the same passage Ibn Kathir gives the Prophet's ﷺ warning against inflation of another kind: *"Do not exaggerate in praising me as ʿIsa bin Maryam was praised upon him be peace and blessings. I am just a servant of Allah. Say, 'He is His servant and Messenger.'"* False parentage and inflated status share one disease: letting words re-describe what Allah has fixed.

## Ayah 6: the bond that is real

*"The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers."*

Ibn Kathir explains this as the Messenger's ﷺ mercy and sincerity toward his Ummah, and **his judgement or ruling takes precedence over their own choices for themselves** — as Allah says, *"But no, by your Lord, they can have no faith, until they make you judge in all disputes between them, and find in themselves no resistance against your decisions, and accept with full submission"* (4:65). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that on this reading — based on the saying of Ibn ʿAtiyyah and others, which al-Qurtubi and most commentators adopted — every Muslim is duty-bound to obey and implement the command of the Prophet ﷺ ahead of the command of his parents; if parents oppose any command of his ﷺ, obeying them in that matter is not permissible. And his command takes precedence even over the pulls of one's own desiring self.

Ibn Kathir cites what is said in the Sahih: *"By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, none of you truly believes until I am dearer to him than his own self, his wealth, his children and all the people."*

And concerning this ayah, al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"There is no believer except I am the closest of all people to him in this world and in the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: 'The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves.' If any believer leaves behind any wealth, let his own relatives inherit it, but if he leaves behind any debt or orphans, bring them to me and I will take care of them."* Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded only by al-Bukhari, who also recorded it in the Book of Loans. His precedence over us is not a claim on our estates; it is his taking responsibility for our debts and our orphans.

## "And his wives are their mothers"

Ibn Kathir explains that the motherhood of the Prophet's ﷺ wives means they are unlawful for marriage; and in terms of honour, respect and veneration, it is not permissible for them to be alone with them. He notes the limit too: the prohibition of marriage to them does not extend to their daughters and sisters, according to scholarly consensus.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses further: theirs is a motherhood in terms of **respect and honour**. The injunctions that ordinarily hold between a mother and her children — the absence of hijab through maḥram status, and shares in inheritance — have nothing to do with it, as the end of the ayah makes explicit. And since the prohibition of marrying them is declared in a separate verse of its own, it is not necessarily grounded in their being "mothers" at all.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a ruling: the least breach of etiquette toward any of the Prophet's ﷺ wives, may Allah be pleased with them, is forbidden, for two reasons — they are the mothers of the Muslim community, and any pain caused to them would cause pain to the Prophet ﷺ, which is forbidden in a far more extreme degree.

## Blood relations and inheritance

*"And blood relations among each other have closer personal ties in the decree of Allah than the believers and the Muhajirin."*

Ibn Kathir explains this as an **abrogation** of the rule that existed previously, whereby they could inherit from one another by virtue of the oath of brotherhood among them. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: "A Muhajir would inherit from an Ansari even though they were not related by blood, because of the brotherhood established between them by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some early commentators read "the believers" here as the Ansar and "the Muhajirin" as the Quraysh, in which case the ayah abrogates inheritance based on the hijrah specifically (al-Qurtubi). It also clears a technical trap: *ulū al-arḥām* here carries its literal sense, covering **all relatives** — including those the jurists call *ʿaṣabāt* (agnates) — and the later juristic terminology that sets *ulū al-arḥām* against *ʿaṣabāt* is not what is meant here.

*"Except that you do kindness to those brothers."* Ibn Kathir: the idea of inheriting from one another has gone, but there remains the duty to offer support and kindness, to uphold ties of brotherhood and to offer good advice. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it concrete: inheritance as such is received only on the basis of relationship, but if you wish to give something to a brother in faith you have the right to do so — as a gift within your lifetime, or by a bequest that reaches him after your death.

*"This has been written in the Book."* Ibn Kathir, giving the view of Mujahid and others, understands this of the First Book, which cannot be altered or changed: the closer tie of blood relatives is a ruling Allah decreed and wrote there. And even though Allah legislated something different at certain times, there is wisdom behind that, for He knew this would be abrogated and the original ruling instituted long ago would prevail. And Allah knows best.

## Living it

- **Names are a trust.** Where a child's lineage is known, it is spoken; where it is unknown, the honest words are brother in faith and *mawlā* — never a borrowed surname.
- **Care is not annulled by correcting the label.** Zayd remained beloved; Salim remained in the household; Hamzah's daughter was placed with those who loved her. The passage removes a fiction, not a family.
- **You are not blamed for what you did not intend** — the accounting is on what the heart deliberately means.
- **The measure of faith is where the Prophet ﷺ stands in your loyalties** — not merely admired, but preferred: over parents, over property, over one's own inclination.

passages.title: The solemn covenant taken from the prophets
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat set before us something very old: a pledge that Allah took from the prophets, and a Day on which He will ask about it. Ayah 7 tells us the covenant was taken; ayah 8 tells us what follows from it — a questioning of the truthful about their truthfulness, and a punishment already prepared for those who rejected them. Together they form one statement: prophethood is not an honour only, it is a trust with a reckoning attached.

## Why this comes here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the thread carefully. At the opening of the sūrah, in the words **«and follow what is revealed to you»**, the Prophet ﷺ was asked to follow the divine revelation sent to him. Then in the previous ayah — **«The Prophet is closer to the believers…»** — the believers were obligated to carry out the orders of the one who receives that revelation. These two ayat, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, restate and reinforce exactly those two points: the recipient of revelation is bound to follow the revelation given to him by Allah, and the one who does not receive revelation is bound to follow the one who does.

So the passage is not a digression into ancient history. It is the deep foundation under the authority the sūrah has just asserted.

## What the covenant was

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here tells us about the five Mighty Messengers with strong resolve and the other prophets, and how He took a covenant from them **to establish the religion of Allah, to convey His Message, and to cooperate and support one another.**

He anchors this in another ayah where the terms of the pledge are spelled out almost verbatim:

> «And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets, saying: "Take whatever I gave you from the Book and Hikmah, and afterwards there will come to you a Messenger confirming what is with you; you must, then, believe in him and help him." Allah said: "Do you agree, and will you take up My covenant?" They said: "We agree." He said: "Then bear witness; and I am with you among the witnesses."» (3:81)

Read that alongside our ayah and the shape of the covenant becomes clear. It is not a vague promise of piety. It has clauses: hold fast to what I have given you; recognise the Messenger who comes after, confirming what you already have; believe in him; help him. And it has a formal ratification — a question, an answer, a call to bear witness, with Allah Himself among the witnesses.

Ibn Kathir adds a second cross-reference, an ayah in which these same five are named, and which shows what they were all commissioned with:

> «He (Allah) has ordained for you the same religion which He ordained for Nuh, and that which We have revealed to you, and that which We ordained for Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa — saying you should establish religion and make no divisions in it.» (42:13)

Ibn Kathir then says plainly: *this* is the covenant which Allah took from them. One religion, one commission, one line of men under the same oath. That is why division in religion cuts so deep: it damages the very thing they were all pledged to establish.

**Qatadah's summary.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports — as Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have reported from Sayyidnā Qatādah — that this pledge from the prophets was a pledge of three things: discharging the duties of prophethood and messengership, attesting to the veracity of one another, and being mutually helpful.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān further notes that according to one narration, the pledge also included that they should proclaim: *Sayyidnā Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ is the Messenger of Allah, and the last of the prophets; after him there will be no prophet.*

## A covenant unique to the prophets

There is a universal pledge taken from the entire creation — the pledge of **«Am I not your Lord?»** (*alastu bi-rabbikum*), taken from the created at large. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say that the covenant in our ayah is **in addition to** that one, and cites a saying of the Prophet ﷺ reported by Imam Ahmad: that it was the prophets *only* from whom the covenant of messengership and prophethood was taken, and that this is the meaning of Allah's words, *"And when We took from the prophets their covenant…"*

So there are two layers. Every soul owes Allah the acknowledgement that He is Lord. The prophets owe that *and* a second, heavier obligation on top of it — the obligation of the ones sent.

**When was it taken?** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and it is worth naming both views rather than flattening them:

- **Ibn Kathir** states that this covenant was taken from them *after their missions started* — that is, in the course of their prophetic careers in this world.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān**, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and Mazharī, holds that this pledge from the prophets was taken **in eternity (*azal*)**, at the same time as the pledge of *alastu bi-rabbikum* was taken from the created at large.

Both readings preserve the same essential point — that the prophets stand under a solemn, willingly accepted obligation. Where they differ is in placing the moment: within history, or before it.

## "A strong covenant"

The ayah does not leave the pledge unqualified: **«We took from them a strong covenant.»** **Ibn ʿAbbās** glossed that phrase simply and directly: *the strong covenant is al-ʿAhd* — the covenant, the given word.

The description is doing work. This is not spoken of as a casual undertaking that circumstances might excuse; it is named as strong, and it was taken from the weightiest of Allah's servants.

## Why the Prophet ﷺ is named first

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes the sequence: after mentioning the prophets in general, peace be upon them all, five are then named particularly, on the basis of the unique distinction they have among the group of prophets. Ibn Kathir likewise identifies these five as the **Mighty Messengers with strong resolve**, named here and in 42:13.

And then the detail that both commentaries pause over. The list runs Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, ʿIsa — but before it begins, Allah says **«and from you»** (*minka*). The mention of the Prophet ﷺ is made to precede that of the others, although, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, his appearance in this world is later than all of them.

Ibn Kathir explains: this ayah begins with the last Prophet ﷺ **as a token of respect**, and then the names of the other prophets are given in order, may the blessings of Allah be upon them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a further reason drawn from a hadith:

> *"I am the first human being in the creation and the last of them in being sent (with the prophetic mission)."*
> — reported by Ibn Saʿd and Abu Nuʿaim in *Al-Hilyah* from Maisirah al-Mafjar, and by At-Tabarani in *al-Kabir* from Ibn ʿAbbās (cited via Mazharī)

Read that way, *minka* is not merely a courtesy of word order. He ﷺ is placed first because in one sense he *is* first — last to appear among men, first in creation. The order of the ayah quietly says something about his rank before it says anything about his mission.

For a reader following the sūrah's argument, this lands with force. The sūrah has just bound the believers to carry out the orders of the one who receives revelation. Now it shows where he stands in the assembly of prophets: named ahead of Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa, in an ayah about the most binding pledge Allah took.

## Ayah 8: the questioning

**«That He may ask the truthful about their truth.»**

The covenant was not taken and then filed away. The ayah moves straight from the pledge to a questioning about it: so that Allah may question these men of truth about their delivery of it.

Who are "the truthful" who will be questioned? Ibn Kathir reports **Mujahid**'s explanation: this refers to **those who convey the Message from the Messengers.** On that reading the questioning reaches past the prophets themselves to those who carried what they brought — everyone standing in the chain of delivery.

Note the sobering shape of the sentence. The ones questioned are *the truthful*, asked about *their truth*. If those with the strongest claim to honesty are still brought forward and asked, no one who handles this religion's message is exempt from being asked what he did with it.

**«And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful torment.»**

Ibn Kathir specifies: the disbelievers here are those **among their nations** — the people to whom these very messengers were sent. And "painful", he glosses as **agonizing**. The verb is telling: the punishment is *prepared*, already made ready.

So ayah 8 sets two futures side by side. The truthful are questioned — and questioning implies a case that can be answered. For the rejecters, in this sentence, something has simply been made ready.

## The verdict already recorded

Ibn Kathir closes with what reads almost as testimony given in advance:

> We bear witness that the Messengers did indeed convey the Message of their Lord and advised their nations, and that they clearly showed them the truth in which there is no confusion, doubt or ambiguity, even though they were rejected by the ignorant, stubborn and rebellious wrongdoers. What the Messengers brought is the truth, and whoever opposes them is misguided.

The outcome of the questioning is not in doubt. The prophets kept the covenant. The clarity was there; what was missing was not evidence but willingness. Ibn Kathir seals it with the words of the people of Paradise:

> «Indeed, the Messengers of our Lord did come with the truth.» (7:43)

That is the last word on the trial — spoken by those who accepted, after everything is over.

## Living it

These are reflections drawn out of the commentary above rather than statements of it; the tafsir's own words are as given.

**Take the chain seriously.** If Mujahid is right that the questioning includes those who convey the Message from the Messengers, then anyone who repeats an ayah, teaches a child, corrects a friend, or forwards a religious claim is standing — however far down — in that line of conveyance. Accuracy in what we pass on is not pedantry; it is covenant-keeping.

**Honour every prophet.** Qatādah's summary includes attesting to the veracity of one another. If the prophets were pledged to affirm each other, then loving Muhammad ﷺ properly sits naturally with honouring Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa, peace be upon them all — men under one shared oath, not rivals.

**Refuse division.** The commission in 42:13 was «establish religion and make no divisions in it». Sectarian fracture is not a side issue; it is the one thing the shared commission explicitly warned against.

**Let the ayah settle the question of authority.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's framing is the practical heart of the passage: the recipient of revelation is bound to follow what Allah revealed to him, and everyone else is bound to follow him. If the Prophet ﷺ himself stands under a strong covenant to deliver, then following his delivery is not optional preference — it is the other half of the same arrangement.

passages.title: The Confederates repelled by wind and angels
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Allah turns to the believers and asks them to remember one particular rescue: the day a coalition of armies encircled Madinah and Allah broke the siege with a wind and with forces no eye could see. Ayat 9–11 move as one arc — the favour is named first (ayah 9), then the terror it rescued them from is described (ayah 10), then the meaning of the whole episode is stated (ayah 11): the believers were tried, and shaken with a mighty shaking. Allah tells them the ending before He makes them relive the middle.

## The event being remembered

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah "tells us of the blessings and favors He bestowed upon His believing servants when He diverted their enemies and defeated them in the year when they gathered together and plotted." That was the year of al-Khandaq — the Trench — in Shawwal of the year 5 AH, which Ibn Kathir calls the well-known correct view, though he notes that Musa bin 'Uqbah and others said it was in the year 4 AH. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places it in the fourth year, adding that some narrations say the fifth.

The battle carries two names. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **al-Aḥzāb** is the plural of *ḥizb*, which means party or group: the combined forces of different groups of disbelievers, bound by a pact to eliminate the Muslims, attacked Madinah together, so the battle took the name of the confederacy itself. And because a trench (*khandaq*) was dug across the enemy's line of attack under the orders of the Prophet ﷺ, it is also called the Battle of the Trench.

**How the coalition was assembled.** Ibn Kathir records that a group of the leaders of the Jews of Banu Nadir — whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had expelled from Madinah to Khaybar — including Sallam bin Abu al-Huqayq, Sallam bin Mishkam and Kinanah bin ar-Rabi', went to Makkah, met the leaders of Quraysh, and incited them to make war against the Prophet ﷺ, promising help and support. Quraysh agreed. They then went to the Ghatafan tribe with the same call, and they responded too.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the conversation. About twenty men from Banu Nadir and the tribe of Abu Wa'il reached Makkah. The Quraysh chiefs doubted that idol-worshippers and People of the Book could find any common ground, so they asked: "You are the people of the Book and the people of learning. First of all, you tell us as to which religion is better in your sight, ours or theirs?" The reply, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, was "totally contrary to their knowledge and conscience" — *your religion is better than the religion of Muhammad* ﷺ. Satisfied, these twenty visitors joined by fifty of the Quraysh chiefs went to al-Masjid al-Ḥaram, clung to the walls of the Baytullah by their chests, and made a solemn pledge before Allah that they would fight against the Prophet ﷺ to their last man.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this a unique manifestation of Allah's forbearance and magnanimity, and notes where that oath ends: every one of them bolted from this battle.

Ghatafan, for its part, was bought. The delegation promised them the total produce of dates in one year at Khaybar — half of it, according to some narrations — and their chief 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn approved his participation on that condition.

**The numbers.** Ibn Kathir reports the coalition as nearly ten thousand: Quraysh under Abu Sufyan Sakhr bin Harb, Ghatafan under 'Uyaynah bin Hisn bin Badr. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts four thousand men out of Makkah with three hundred horses and war supplies laden on a thousand camels, joined at Marr az-Zahran by Aslam, Ashja', Banu Murrah, Banu Kinanah, Fazarah and Ghatafan — the total reported as ten thousand in some narrations, twelve thousand in others, fifteen thousand in still others. Against them stood three thousand Muslims — Ibn Kathir notes it was also said they numbered seven hundred — with thirty-six horses between them, very ill-equipped, and the time was hard winter. Badr had faced one thousand; Uhud three thousand. This was the largest force ever brought against them, which is why Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it the severest battle the Prophet ﷺ and the noble Sahabah endured.

## The trench, and where trust belongs

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that when news of this aggressive united front reached the Prophet ﷺ, his very first verbal reaction was the words of the Qur'an: *Allah is all-sufficient for us, and the best One to trust in* (3:173). Then he assembled the opinion leaders from among the Muhajirin and the Ansar and went into consultation with them — although, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the recipient of revelation really needs no consultation, since he acts directly with the permission of Allah. There were two advantages in it: to establish consultation as a practice in the Muslim community, and to revive mutual bonds and unity among the believers.

Present among the consultants was Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, who had recently freed himself from slavery under a Jewish master and devoted himself to the service of Islam. He advised that in his country the Persian kings had trenches dug across the enemy's line of attack, and it had always helped stop them. The Prophet ﷺ accepted the advice and ordered the digging — and participated in it himself. Ibn Kathir says the Muslims did this, working hard, "and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ worked with them, carrying earth away and digging, in the process of which there occurred many miracles and clear signs."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the layout: the trench was dug along the whole passageway behind the mount of Salʿ, the route the enemy could use to enter Madinah from the north, beginning at Shaykhayn and reaching the western corner of Salʿ, later extended to the intersection of the valleys of Buthan and Rana — approximately three and a half miles in total. The ground marking of its length and width was drawn personally by the Prophet ﷺ. The whole army was divided into groups of ten men, each group responsible for forty yards.

**"Salman is part of our family."** Because Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, was the one who had advised the digging, knew the job, was strong, and was neither of the Ansar nor of the Muhajirin, a sort of competition arose between the two groups, each wanting him with them — until the Prophet ﷺ intervened to avoid a dispute and gave his verdict: *Salmān minnā ahl al-bayt*, "Salman is part of our family." The universal habit in our time, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, is that people do not like to treat the non-local as their equal; here every group felt proud to have the competent man on their side.

**The rock and the three strikes.** In the section of the trench entrusted to Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, a huge, hard and glossy rock showed up. His colleague Sayyidna 'Amr Ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, says: "This rock broke our implements and we failed to cut it apart." He suggested that although the trench could be dug around the rock with a minor crookedness, they should not depart from the line the Prophet ﷺ had drawn on the strength of their own opinion — so Salman should go and ask.

Salman found the Prophet ﷺ working in his own part of the trench, hauling out the dug earth. Sayyidna Bara' Ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him, says: "I saw him. Dust had covered his blessed body in a manner that the skin on his front and back was not visible." Rather than send back an instruction, he came in person, went down into the trench and joined the diggers. He took the pickaxe in his blessed hands, struck the rock and recited *tammat kalimatu rabbika ṣidqā* — "And the Word of your Lord is perfect in truth" (6:115). One third of the rock was cut away, and a streak of light was released from it. He struck again, reciting the verse further — *ṣidqan wa 'adlā*, "in truth and justice" — and another third came away with another streak of light. The third strike finished it.

Then he came out, picked up the sheet wrap he had left at the trench's edge and sat down. Salman said, "Y Rasulallah, every time you struck at the rock, I saw a light coming out of it." The Prophet ﷺ asked whether he had really seen it, and Salman said, "I have seen it with my own eyes." The Prophet ﷺ told him: in the light released after the first strike he saw the palaces of the cities of Yaman and those of Cyrus, and the angel Jibra'il told him, "your Ummah will conquer these cities"; at the second strike he was shown the red palaces of the Byzantines, with the same good news. Having heard this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, all the Muslims felt at peace and became assured of their great successes in the future.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a fine observation. Along that three and a half mile stretch, no one among the diggers faced an obstacle that left him helpless — except Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, the very man whose advice had begun the project. Allah showed him that even after digging a perfect trench there was no way out except turning to Allah for help when every tool and instrument failed. These blessed souls were being taught that assembling material means to the measure of one's capacity and ability is obligatory, but placing trust in those means is not correct. The believer's trust — even after assembling every possible means — should be in Allah alone.

## "From above you and from below you"

Ibn Kathir explains that the idolators camped to the north of Madinah, near Uhud, and some of them camped on the high ground overlooking Madinah — that is *from above you*. And *from below you*, he explains through the report from Abu Hudhayfah, refers to Banu Qurayzah: a group among the Jews who had a fortress in the south-east of Madinah and numbered nearly eight hundred fighters. They had made a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ and were under his protection — until Huyay bin Akhtab an-Nadari went to them and kept working on them until they broke the treaty and went over to the side of the Confederates. That is when, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the crisis deepened and things got worse."

The believers had their backs towards the mountain of Salʿ and were facing the enemy, with the ditch — in which there was no water — between the two groups, preventing the cavalry and infantry from reaching them. The women and children were in the strongholds of Madinah.

The siege lasted almost a month with no fighting between them, except when 'Amr bin 'Abd Wadd al-'Amiri, one of the most famous and bravest horsemen of the Jahiliyyah, came with some other horsemen and crossed the ditch to the Muslim side. Ibn Kathir reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called for the Muslim cavalry, and it was said that no one came forward; then he called 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who came forward, and they fought in single combat until 'Ali killed him — and this, Ibn Kathir says, was a sign of imminent victory.

## "The eyes grew wild and the hearts reached to the throats"

On these words Ibn Kathir's comment: this "means, from intense fear and terror."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same two phrases as "the eyes were distracted" and "hearts reached the throats," and lists them together with "they were shaken with a violent convulsion" from ayah 11 as the way the Qur'an itself describes "the horrible severity of this event."

Ibn Kathir sums up ayah 11: when the Confederates surrounded Madinah and the Muslims were besieged and found themselves in straitened circumstances, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in their midst, "they were tried and tested, and were shaken with a mighty shaking. At this time hypocrisy emerged, and those in whose hearts was a disease spoke about what they really felt."

## "And you were harbouring doubts about Allah"

The commentators Ibn Kathir gathers read this phrase in more than one way:

- **Ibn Jarir** said: "Some of those who were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had doubts and thought that the outcome would be against the believers, and that Allah would allow that to happen."
- **Muhammad bin Ishaq** said the believers had all kinds of doubts, and hypocrisy emerged to such an extent that Mu'attib bin Qushayr, the brother of Banu 'Amr bin 'Awf, said: "Muhammad was promising us that we would win the treasure of Chosroes and Caesar, but one of us cannot even go and relieve himself."
- **Al-Hasan** distinguished the two camps sharply: "There were different kinds of thoughts; the hypocrites thought that Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions would be eliminated, while the believers were certain that what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ promised was true, and that He would cause the religion to prevail even if the idolators hated it."

## The night of the wind

Ayah 9 names two instruments plainly: *a wind, and forces that you saw not*.

**The wind.** Ibn Kathir: "Then Allah sent an intensely cold wind with strong gusts against the Confederates, and they were left with no tents or anything else; they could not light any fires or do anything, and so they departed, disappointed and defeated." Mujahid said this was the easterly wind — a view Ibn Kathir supports with words of the Prophet ﷺ: "I was given victory by the easterly wind, and 'Ad were destroyed by the westerly wind." (The source reports these words without naming the collection that records them.)

**The forces you did not see.** Ibn Kathir explains that this "refers to the angels who shook them and cast fear and terror into their hearts." He describes the result: the chief of each tribe called out, "O Banu so-and-so, to me!" So they gathered around him, and he said, "Let us save ourselves," when Allah cast fear and terror into their hearts.

Ibn Kathir preserves that night through one man's eyes. **In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded** that Ibrahim at-Taymi said that his father said: we were with Hudhayfah bin al-Yaman, may Allah be pleased with him, and a man said to him, "If I had met the Messenger of Allah ﷺ I would have fought alongside him and I would have striven my utmost." Hudhayfah said to him: "Would you really have done that? I was present with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during the campaign against the Confederates on a very cold and windy night," and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Is there any man who will bring me news of the people? He will be with me on the Day of Resurrection." None of us answered him, and he repeated it a second and a third time. Then he ﷺ said: "O Hudhayfah, get up and bring us news of the people." When he called me by name, I had no choice but to get up. He said: "Bring us news of the people, but do not alarm them." So I went, walking as if I were walking among pigeons, until I came to them. I saw Abu Sufyan warming his back by the fire, and I put an arrow in my bow, wanting to shoot it at him — then I remembered what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *Do not alarm them.* If I had shot the arrow, I would have hit him. So I came back the same way. After my return I began to feel very cold. I told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he gave me to wear a spare cloak of his which he used to pray in. I slept until morning came, and when morning came he said: "Get up, O sleepy one!"

These men were not without fear; they were so drained that even the promise of the Prophet's ﷺ company on the Day of Resurrection could not lift them, until one was named and rose anyway. And the night ends with the Prophet ﷺ wrapping a freezing man in his own praying cloak and waking him with a joke.

## A du'a for a throat-tight heart

Ibn Kathir records that **Ibn Abi Hatim** reported from Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him: "On the day of al-Khandaq, we said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there anything we should say, for our hearts have reached our throats?' He ﷺ said: 'Yes, say: *O Allah, cover our weak points and calm our fears.*'" Then Allah struck the faces of the enemy with the wind and defeated them with the wind. Ibn Kathir adds that this was also recorded by Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal from Abu 'Amir al-'Aqadi.

## What the passage asks of us

**Remember on command.** Ayah 9 does not say "be grateful" in the abstract; it says *remember* — call to mind, deliberately, this specific rescue with its date and its details. Faith is kept alive by refusing to forget particular mercies.

**Do the digging, then rely on Allah.** Three and a half miles of trench were dug, groups of ten organised, boys under fifteen sent home, standards assigned separately to the Muhajirin and the Ansar for administrative order — and then a rock no tool could break taught them the lesson. The Prophet's ﷺ own first words on hearing the news were *Allah is all-sufficient for us, and the best One to trust in*.

**Expect the shaking.** Ayah 11 is not an accusation but a description: *there the believers were tried and shaken with a mighty shaking*. Being shaken is not the failure. Al-Hasan's line marks the fork: under identical pressure the hypocrite concluded that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions would be eliminated, while the believer stayed certain that what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ promised was true.

**Allah's help does not need to be visible to be real.** The forces Allah sent were, in the Qur'an's own words, forces *you saw not*. What the believers saw was a cold night and, by morning, an empty plain. Ayah 9 closes with the reminder that Allah is Ever All-Seer of what you do. Those forces were unseen by them; nothing about them was unseen by Him.

passages.title: The hypocrites' excuses during the siege
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take us inside Madinah while the city is under siege, and let us hear what the hypocrites were actually saying — first their sneer at Allah's promise, then their two ways of walking off the line, then Allah's verdict on what was really in their hearts, and finally the reminder of the pledge they had already broken. What holds the passage together is a single movement: from **words** (ayah 12), to **excuses** (ayah 13), to the **hidden truth beneath both** (ayah 14), to the **covenant that will be asked about** (ayah 15).

## The moment being described

Ibn Kathir sets the scene: "Allah tells us what happened when the Confederates surrounded Al-Madinah and the Muslims were besieged and found themselves in straitened circumstances, with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in their midst. They were tried and tested, and were shaken with a mighty shaking. At this time hypocrisy emerged, and those in whose hearts was a disease spoke about what they really felt."

The pressure was extraordinary. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes some three thousand ill-equipped defenders facing an equipped army of ten to twelve thousand. The trench itself — about three and a half miles — had been dug in six days, ten men to every ten yards, by men who had no servants to dig for them and who worked with their own hands in a lashing winter; those who finished their stretch early went to help others still digging. Then came the news that Banu Quraizah, bound to the Prophet ﷺ by a standing peace treaty, had broken it and joined the Confederates. That was the crisis: the trench held back the armies coming from outside, but Banu Quraizah were *inside* Madinah.

*(A note on scope: the words "from above you and from below you" belong to ayah 10, just before our passage. Maʿārif reports that tafsir authorities explain "above" as Banu Quraizah and "below" as the rest of the Confederates. I mention it only because it names the exact pressure the men of ayat 12 and 13 were reacting to.)*

Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, said she had been with the Prophet ﷺ at Muraysiʿ, Khaybar, Hudaybiyah, the conquest of Makkah and Hunayn, and that none of them was as hard on him as Khandaq: more wounds, the severity of the winter chill, and food and water desperately short. On one day of continuous arrow-fire the Muslims could not find a moment for Salah, and four prayers of the day had to be performed at the time of ʿIshaʾ. This is the atmosphere in which the sentences of ayat 12 and 13 were spoken.

## Ayah 12 — "Nothing but delusion"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the specific occasion. While the trench was being dug, hypocrites working alongside the Muslims began needling them: is it not strange, they said, that Muhammad tells you he can see the palaces of Hirah in the south and Madaʾin in the north from the depth of this ditch being dug in Yathrib — and that *you* will conquer them? Look at yourselves: digging and digging, forgetful of all your needs, without even the time to take care of your human compulsions. And you are going to conquer the countries of Cyrus and others? It was about this very event, Maʿārif says, that ayah 12 was revealed: **"Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion."** Maʿārif renders the same words as, "Allah and His messenger did not promise us but deceitfully."

Notice what the accusation attacks. Not the Prophet's ﷺ strategy — his *promise*, and behind it Allah's promise. Maʿārif sums up what they were claiming: that the promises of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ "were a web of deception." And it names what the outburst really was: "an externalized demonstration of their inner disbelief."

On the two descriptions in the ayah — "the hypocrites" and "those in whose hearts is a disease" — the sources before us do not read the phrase identically, and it is worth letting that stand rather than smoothing it over. Ibn Kathir comments in one continuous sentence: "Their hypocrisy became apparent, while the one in whose heart was doubt became weak, and he expressed the ideas that were in his heart because of the weakness of his faith and the difficulty of the situation." Maʿārif, glossing the second phrase directly, says that "reference is being made to the state of the same hypocrites hidden in whose hearts there was that disease of hypocrisy." On either reading the mechanism described is the same: hardship did not create what was inside them; it brought it out into speech. A siege is a kind of x-ray.

**And the contrast is the point of the passage.** Maʿārif is careful here, and it draws the contrast using ayah 10 — one ayah earlier than our passage, but part of the same siege account. Of the believers ayah 10 says, "and you were thinking about Allah all sorts of thoughts." Maʿārif explains that these were scruples that emerge in a person's heart beyond his control at a time of acute anxiety, when one may feel death as near with no hope of deliverance left, and that "such non-voluntary apprehensions and scruples are neither contradictory of the perfection of ʾĪmān (faith) nor that of one's nearness to Allah" — they only point to the severity of the distress, since such scruples crept even into the hearts of the noble Sahabah, who were otherwise "virtual mountains of fortitude."

That distinction is worth carrying with you. An unbidden fear that visits a believing heart is not the disease of ayah 12. The disease is when the tongue turns that pressure into an accusation against Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Maʿārif marvels at the sincere ones precisely on this point: with every visible cause and condition running against them, they "did not have the least doubt or qualm of conscience about what the Holy Prophet ﷺ had told them" — and that, it says, is why the value of faith is the highest of all deeds.

## Ayah 13 — two ways of leaving

Maʿārif notes that from here the Qurʾan mentions **two groups** of hypocrites who were part of the Jihad effort along with the Muslims, though outwardly only.

**The first group left without asking.** They called out, "O people of Yathrib! There is no position for you, so go back." Ibn Kathir glosses *lā muqāma lakum* as: "here, with the Prophet ﷺ, you cannot stand guard" — and *fa-rjiʿū*, "go back," as "to your houses and dwellings." Maʿārif says of this group simply that they "started running without any permission." It is a public unravelling of morale: not a private wobble but a shout down the line telling men at their posts that the position is untenable.

It is also worth pausing on the name they used. Ibn Kathir explains "O people of Yathrib" as meaning Al-Madinah, and cites what "was reported in the Sahih": the Prophet ﷺ said, *"I was shown in a dream the place to which you will migrate, a land between two lava fields. At first I thought it was Hajar, but it turned out to be Yathrib"* — another narration having "Al-Madinah." Ibn Kathir then relays from As-Suhayli that the name Yathrib is traced to a man of the ʿAmāliq who settled there, and that it was narrated from some of them that the city is given eleven names in the Tawrah: Al-Madinah, Tābah, Tayyibah, Al-Miskīnah, Al-Jābirah, Al-Muhibbah, Al-Mahbūbah, Al-Qāsimah, Al-Majbūrah, Al-ʿAdhrāʾ and Al-Marhūmah. A city carrying that many names of blessing is being addressed by these men with its bare old one.

**The second group asked to be excused.** "A band of them ask permission of the Prophet, saying: 'Truly, our homes lie open.'" Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that these were Banu Harithah, who said, "We fear for our homes, that they may be robbed" — and Ibn Kathir notes this was also stated by others, while Ibn Ishaq mentioned the one who said it as ʿAws bin Qayzī.

Ibn Kathir explains the plea itself: they were using as an excuse to go back to their houses the claim that the houses "were lying open and had nothing to protect them from the enemy, so they were afraid for their homes." Maʿārif renders their words as, "In fact our homes are vulnerable." It is the perfect excuse, because it is not cowardice; it is *responsibility*. Who could fault a man for worrying about his wife and children behind an unguarded wall?

Then comes one of the most striking short sentences in the Qurʾan: **wa mā hiya bi-ʿawrah** — "and they lay not open." Ibn Kathir: "it is not as they claim." Allah simply contradicts the fact they had asserted. And He states the motive they had not stated: *in yurīdūna illā firāran*, "They but wished to flee" — Ibn Kathir: "they wanted to run away from the battlefield." Maʿārif puts it bluntly: "the Qurʾan exposed the hollowness of their excuses as a pack of lies. The truth of the matter was no more than that they intended to run from the battlefront."

Note the grammar of the exposure. The excuse is quoted in their own voice; the correction is Allah's. A man can construct a reason so tidy that no human commander can refuse it — and Allah, who does not need to interrogate anyone, names the thing the reason was built to hide.

## Ayah 14 — what they would have done

Ayah 14 pushes past what they *did* to what they *were*. Ibn Kathir explains: if the enemy had entered upon them from every side of Al-Madinah and from every direction, and had then demanded that they become disbelievers, "they would have promptly done so. They would not have adhered to their faith or remained steadfast in it if they were faced with the slightest fear." He notes: "This is how it was interpreted by Qatadah, ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd and Ibn Jarir," and comments: "This is a condemnation of them in the clearest terms."

So the *fitnah* they would have been exhorted to is, on this reading, the abandonment of faith itself — a demand that they become disbelievers. And the sting is in the last clause: they "would have hesitated thereupon but little." They would barely have paused. Men who could not stand a cold month behind a trench would not have stood one demand at the gate.

This tells us what a false excuse actually is. It is never only about the one occasion. Ayah 13 shows a lie about a wall; ayah 14 shows the wall was never the issue.

## Ayah 15 — the covenant that will be asked about

Then, Ibn Kathir says, "Allah reminds them of the promise they had made to Him before this fear struck them, that they would not turn their backs or flee from the battlefield." That is the force of ayah 15: whatever they were saying now, there had been a pledge earlier, made when the sky was clear.

And on **wa kāna ʿahdu llāhi masʾūlā** — "a covenant with Allah must be answered for" — Ibn Kathir writes: "Allah will inevitably ask them about that covenant." The passive construction leaves the questioner unnamed and therefore unmistakable. A commitment made to Allah does not lapse because circumstances became inconvenient; it becomes a question waiting for you.

### Where the argument goes next (ayat 16–17 — just outside our four)

Our passage ends at ayah 15, but Ibn Kathir carries the thought straight on into the two ayat that follow, and knowing where it lands makes ayah 15 land harder. He explains that fleeing from battle "will not delay their appointed demise or make their lives any longer; on the contrary, it may be the cause of their being taken sooner, and in a sudden manner" — and that even if flight bought something, "you will enjoy no more than a little while." He brings alongside it the words of Allah, "Say: 'Short is the enjoyment of this world. The Hereafter is better for him who has Taqwa'" (4:77). And on the question of who could shield them from Allah: "they have no one else except Allah to respond to their cries." The whole calculation of the deserter collapses. The thing he ran to save was never his to keep, and the One he ran from is the only refuge there is.

## Background: two scenes from the wider siege account

Because these ayat name a failure, it helps to see one contrasting scene from the same battle. This belongs to the broader Khandaq narrative in Maʿārif rather than to the commentary on ayat 12–15 themselves, so I keep it short.

When the strain was at its worst, the Prophet ﷺ explored offering the Ghatafan chiefs a third of Madinah's fruit to withdraw — and, as was his habit, consulted. Saʿd bin Muʿadh and Saʿd bin ʿUbadah asked whether this was a command from Allah, his personal opinion, or a measure to save them from the hardship. He ﷺ answered: "Neither is there a Divine order for it, nor do I have any personal inclination to do so. In fact, I have come up with this via media in view of your pain and suffering because you are surrounded from all sides." Saʿd bin Muʿadh then said that when they worshipped idols and knew nothing of Allah, these people could not dare look at a single fruit of the city with greedy eyes except as guests or buyers — "Today, when Allah Taʿālā has, in His infinite grace, given us the ability of knowing Him, and has bestowed upon us the honour of Islam, shall we, on this day, let these people have our fruits and our wealth and our properties?... we are not going to give them anything but the cutting edge of our swords." The Prophet ﷺ set the idea aside, and Saʿd erased the unsigned document. Set that answer beside "our homes lie open."

And on a freezing night, when the Prophet ﷺ asked three times for a man to bring back news of the enemy camp with Jannah as the reward, the Companions were so broken by cold, hunger and fatigue that none could rise; he then called Hudhayfah bin al-Yamān by name. Hudhayfah's account — which Maʿārif notes appears in the Sahih of Muslim — is that he stood while his whole body shivered, and that once he set out he felt as though he were walking inside a hot bath the whole way. The difference between him and the men of ayah 13 is not that he felt no fear or no cold. It is what he did while feeling it.

## Living it

**Watch the moment pressure makes you talk.** Ayah 12 is not condemning fear; it is condemning the sentence that turns fear into a charge against Allah's promise. Maʿārif's ruling on the believers' own dread (at ayah 10) is a mercy here: the involuntary scruples that grip a heart in a crisis contradict neither the perfection of faith nor a person's nearness to Allah.

**Be suspicious of the excuse that flatters you.** The most dangerous excuses are the ones that sound like duty — my family, my home, my responsibilities. Ayah 13 is a permanent warning that a reason can be entirely presentable and still be, as Allah says of theirs, simply not true.

**Keep the pledges you made in easy weather.** Ayah 15 is the whole of it: you made the covenant before the fear struck, and "a covenant with Allah must be answered for."

**And carry the Prophet's ﷺ own example from those days.** Commenting on this same passage, Maʿārif points out that the Sahabah never wanted him to do the hard labour of digging with them; it was his own initiative to share it, "to mollify their hearts and teach them their essential lesson to put mutual brotherhood to practice." In that trench there was no ruler and no one being ruled, no king and no subject. From the time those in power abandoned that Sunnah, Maʿārif warns, is when such differences gushed forth, bringing all sorts of tests and trials in their wake.

passages.title: Flight from death will not save you
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are one continuous argument, delivered to the men inside Madinah who were looking for a way out while the Confederate armies were at the city. Allah gives His Prophet ﷺ two questions to put to them — *what exactly does running buy you?* and *who is it that can put you beyond Allah's reach?* — and then draws a precise portrait of the people asking to leave: what they whisper to their friends, how their eyes look when danger arrives, how their tongues sound once it has passed, and how the fear stays with them even after the enemy has gone.

One thread runs through all five: **there is no exit from Allah's decree, so the only real question is where you would rather be standing when it comes.**

## The setting

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene briefly. The hypocrites had begun openly saying that "Allah and His messenger did not promise us but deceitfully" (ayah 12) — what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls an externalised demonstration of their inner disbelief. Two groups who were part of the war effort in outward form only then peeled away: one simply left, calling "O people of Yathrib (Madinah), there is no place for you to stay; so go back" (ayah 13); the other asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to withdraw, pleading that "our homes are vulnerable" — an excuse the Qur'an itself dismantled, *while they were not vulnerable*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the pretext a pack of lies; the truth was only **"they wanted nothing but to escape"** (ayah 13).

And Ibn Kathir notes that these were men who had already given Allah a promise, before the fear arrived, that they would not turn their backs and flee the battlefield — a covenant, in his words, that **"Allah will inevitably ask them about."**

Their pledge is on record. Their excuse has been taken apart. Ayah 16 is where the argument begins.

## Two questions that close every exit (16–17)

**"Say: 'Flight will not avail you if you flee from death or killing… and then you will enjoy no more than a little while.'"**
**"Say: 'Who is he who can protect you from Allah if He intends to harm you, or intends mercy on you?'"**

Both ayat open with the same command — *Say* — and they work as a pair. The first dismantles their plan on its own practical terms; the second removes the ground it was standing on.

Notice that Allah does not begin by calling them cowards. He begins by showing them that escape does not achieve what they think it achieves. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: fleeing from battle **"will not delay their appointed demise or make their lives any longer; on the contrary, it may be the cause of their being taken sooner, and in a sudden manner."**

That last clause deserves a pause. The flight they imagined as self-preservation may be the very road to a quicker and more startling end. The man who runs from the appointed hour does not outrun it; he may simply meet it somewhere less honourable.

There is a deliberate echo in the wording. Ayah 13 had already named their motive — *in yurīdūna illā firāran*, "they wanted nothing but to escape." Now ayah 16 takes that same word, *al-firār*, flight, and puts it in the opening clause: *flight will not avail you*. The Qur'an states their motive, then three ayat later tells them it does not work.

And what if it did work? Ibn Kathir explains **"and then you will enjoy no more than a little while"** as what happens *after* the running: even a successful escape has purchased only a brief enjoyment. He sets another ayah beside it to make the scale visible — *"Say: 'Short is the enjoyment of this world. The Hereafter is better for him who has taqwā'"* (4:77), taqwā being the awareness that keeps a person mindful of Allah. The bargain on offer is a handful of days in exchange for a covenant with Allah.

Then ayah 17 moves from strategy to the bedrock question: where can a person stand that is outside Allah's reach? It is asked rhetorically because it has no answer.

Two things are worth noticing. First, the ayah names **both** directions — harm and mercy. For a rebuke it would have been enough to say that nobody can shield you if Allah wills you harm. But the ayah adds: nor can anyone block Allah if He wills you mercy. That is the same truth read from the hopeful side. The One whose decree you cannot escape is also the One whose mercy no army, no siege, and no circumstance can keep from reaching you.
