He records Saʿid bin Jubayr's saying that whoever fasts Ramadan and three days of each month is included in this phrase of the ayah. And he notes that fasting is one of the greatest means of overcoming one's desires, quoting the Prophet's ﷺ counsel to young men: whoever among them can afford to marry should marry, for it is most effective in lowering the gaze and protecting chastity, and whoever cannot should fast, for it will be a protection for him.

**9. The men and women who guard their chastity.** Ibn Kathir says it is quite apt that this should be mentioned next — fasting was just named as the protection, and now comes what is being protected. The meaning is that they protect themselves from forbidden and sinful things, except for what is permitted, as Allah says: *"And those who guard their chastity, except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess — for they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors"* (70:29–31).

**10. The men and women who remember Allah much.** This is remembrance with the hearts and the tongues both. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abi Hatim, from Abu Saʿid Al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said that if a man wakes his wife at night and the two of them pray two rakʿahs, they will be recorded that night among the men and the women who remember Allah much — recorded also, Ibn Kathir notes, by Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Abu Saʿid and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both. Worth pausing over: the description is earned here by a husband and wife together, at night, in two rakʿahs.

He also records from Imam Ahmad, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ was walking along a road in Makkah and came to the mountain of Jumdan and said: "This is Jumdan; go ahead, for the *mufarridūn* have gone ahead." They asked who the *mufarridūn* were, and he ﷺ said: *"The men and the women who remember Allah much."* Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim also recorded it, except for the last part of it. The picture is of travellers on a road with some already far ahead — and the ones out in front are simply those who remember Allah much.

## Why *this* act is the one commanded "much"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to walk past. Islam, it says, stands on five acts of worship — Salah, Zakah, fasting, Hajj and Jihad — yet there is no injunction in the entire Qur'an commanding any one of these to be done *abundantly*. (That enumeration is Maʿārif's own wording; the point it is pressing concerns the command to do something abundantly, not a re-listing of the pillars.) The remembrance of Allah, by heart or tongue, is ordered abundantly in several places, including Surah Al-Anfal (8:45), Surah Al-Jumuʿah (62:10), and here in this ayah.

Why? Maʿārif gives two reasons.

First, dhikr is the essential spirit of all acts of worship. It cites a narration of Muʿadh Ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: someone asked the Prophet ﷺ which of the fighters deserves the best of returns, and he ﷺ said, the one who makes the dhikr of Allah most abundantly; and which of the fasting people is most reward-worthy — the one who makes the dhikr of Allah most abundantly; and similar questions were asked about Salah, Zakah, Hajj and charity, and every time the answer was the same. (Maʿārif attributes the report to Ahmad, via Ibn Kathir.) In other words, dhikr is not merely one more item on the list of ten; it is what the other acts of worship carry within them.

Second, it is the easiest of all acts of worship, and the Shariʿah has placed no condition on it: with wudu' or without, lying down, sitting, or walking, at all times. It demands no hard labour and no formal free time. And yet, Maʿārif says, so great is its effect that even worldly chores transform into worship through it. This is why the Prophet ﷺ taught prayers for before and after eating, for going out and coming back, for before travel, during it and on returning home, and before and after starting a business. The outcome of that whole treasure of prophetic prayers is that no Muslim should do anything at any time while heedless of Allah — and if a person makes these part of the fabric of daily work, then *dunya becomes deen*: worldly duties begin to release the fragrance of faith.

## Living it

Ten qualities — outward submission, inward faith, quiet obedience, honest speech, endurance under blows, humility before the One who sees, open-handedness, discipline of the body, guarded chastity, and a tongue and heart that keep returning to Allah — and every one of them named for men and for women alike. Any believer reading the list can find the one that is thinnest in them and start there.

And the ayah closes by handing all ten the same promise: *"Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward."* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us that for all of those mentioned in this ayah, He has prepared forgiveness of their sins and a great reward — meaning Paradise. Note the verb *prepared*: it is already done, waiting. Forgiveness of sins comes first, and then a reward that Allah describes simply as *great*.

The woman who asked whether her worship was being counted received an answer that has been recited in every generation since. Her question was honoured, not deflected — and the shape of the answer speaks for itself: ten times over, no one left out.

passages.title: Zaynab's marriage and the seal of prophethood
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take one household matter in Madinah and turn it into a permanent principle: once Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have decided something, a believer no longer has a private opinion in it. Ayah 36 lays down the rule; ayat 37–38 show the Prophet ﷺ held to it in his own marriage to Zaynab bint Jaḥsh; ayah 39 describes prophets as men who fear no one but Allah; ayah 40 cuts the root of the custom behind the difficulty — adopted sonship — and seals prophethood with Muhammad ﷺ.

## The story behind ayah 36

Zayd ibn Ḥārithah had been someone's slave. The Prophet ﷺ bought him in the days of Jāhiliyyah at the bazaar of ʿUkāẓ, freed him, and — following the Arab custom of the time — adopted him as his son, so that in Makkah he was called Zayd ibn Muḥammad. When the Qurʼān declared that custom an error of Jāhiliyyah and ordered, "Call them by the name of their real fathers" (33:5), the Companions began attributing him to Ḥārithah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that no Companion is named anywhere in the Qurʼān except Zayd ibn Ḥārithah: severed from attribution to the Prophet ﷺ, he was deprived of a great personal honour, and Allah compensated him by naming him in His Book.

Ibn Kathīr, from Imām Aḥmad, records ʿĀʼishah (may Allah be pleased with her) saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ never sent him on a campaign without appointing him its commander, and that had he outlived him he would have appointed him his khalīfah.

When Zayd came of age, the Prophet ﷺ chose for him **Zaynab bint Jaḥsh**, the daughter of his own paternal aunt. The proposal was refused: because Zayd carried the label of a freed slave, Zaynab and her brother ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh held that they were nobler than him in family and lineage. Ayah 36 came down upon that refusal; they withdrew their objection, the marriage was solemnised, and the Prophet ﷺ paid the dower on Zayd's behalf. According to the majority of commentators this is the well-known occasion of the verse's revelation (Ibn Kathīr, Qurṭubī, Mazharī).

## Julaybīb

Ibn Kathīr and some other commentators report further incidents said likewise to lie behind the verse; Maʿārif observes that several events of this nature may together have been the cause. One is the incident of Julaybīb (may Allah be pleased with him), recorded by Imām Aḥmad from Abū Barzah al-Aslamī.

No man of the Anṣār then would arrange a marriage for a female relative before finding out whether the Prophet ﷺ wanted to marry her himself. So when the Prophet ﷺ said to one of the Anṣār, **"Give me your daughter for marriage,"** the man answered that it would be an honour and a blessing — until the Prophet ﷺ said, **"I do not want her for myself... For Julaybīb."** The girl's mother, delighted a moment earlier, said on hearing the name, "What! Julaybīb? No, by Allah, we will not marry her to him." Then the girl, from her seclusion, asked who was proposing, and said: **"Are you refusing to follow the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ? Follow his command, for I will not come to any harm."** Her father went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "Deal with her as you wish," and he married her to Julaybīb. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentions in *al-Istīʿāb* that this ayah was revealed when the girl said those words.

## The rule itself

Ibn Kathīr insists the ayah is **general in meaning and applies to all matters**: if Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have decreed a matter, no one has any choice or room for personal opinion in it. When Ṭāwūs asked Ibn ʿAbbās about praying two rakʿahs after ʿAṣr and was told not to, Ibn ʿAbbās recited this very ayah. Ibn Kathīr links it to *"But no, by your Lord, they can have no faith, until they make you judge in all disputes between them"* (4:65) — hence the severity: *"And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, he has indeed strayed into a plain error."* Maʿārif draws the legal edge: when the Prophet ﷺ orders someone to do a thing as an obligation, it becomes obligatory for that person **even if the act was not obligatory in its origin**.

**Then what about matching in marriage?** Maʿārif is candid that lineal homogeneity between spouses is desirable even in the sight of the Sharīʿah — so why was their excuse not accepted?

Maʿārif reports a ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ said that girls' marriages should always be arranged through their guardians, and that they should be solemnised within their *kufʼ* (matching) — and states its standing plainly: **"Though, the authority of this Hadith is weak but, with the support from the reports and sayings of the noble Sahabah, it becomes worth being used as an argument."**

So the principle is real but graded. **Matching in religion** is required for the validity of the marriage: a Muslim woman's marriage to a disbeliever is not lawful by the consensus of the ummah even if she agrees — it is the right of Allah. **Matching in wealth** is the woman's own right, hers to drop. **Matching in lineage** is the right of the woman *and* her guardians together; if all of them surrender it for some weightier benefit, they may — and if the benefit is religious, surrendering it is "most desirable and praiseworthy."

Above all this stands *"The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves"* (33:6): his right over his ummah exceeds their right over their own selves. So when he ﷺ ordered Zaynab and ʿAbdullāh to set aside their claim to lineal parity, their duty was to bypass their personal opinion and their own rights.

And *kafāʼah* is no licence to look down on anyone. **In Islam the criterion of low and high is taqwā and love for one's faith; whoever lacks that has no status in the sight of Allah, however noble his family.**

## Ayah 37: the verse he would have hidden

Zaynab stayed with Zayd about a year, and then problems arose. Zayd complained of the sharpness of her tongue and the airs she assumed from her inborn lineal nobility. The Prophet ﷺ had already been informed by revelation that Zayd would divorce her and that she would then be married to him.

When Zayd showed his intention to divorce, the Prophet ﷺ told him, **"Stay with your wife and have Taqwa of Allah"** (Ibn Kathīr). Maʿārif gives two reasons he restrained him. First, divorce, though permissible in the Sharīʿah, is the most detested of permissible things; and the fact that something is destined to happen does not alter the religio-legal ruling that governs our choices. Second, a thought had crossed his blessed heart: if Zayd divorced her and she was then married to him, the Arabs would taunt him, in line with their custom of Jāhiliyyah, that he had married the wife of his son. The Qurʼān had already demolished that custom earlier in this sūrah, so no believer had any scruple left — but disbelievers would still come out with their taunts.

Then came what Maʿārif calls **an endearing reprimand from Allah**: *"And you were concealing in your heart what Allah was going to reveal, and you were fearing people, while Allah is more entitled to be feared by you."*

And he conveyed the very verse that criticised him. Ibn Jarīr narrates from ʿĀʼishah (may Allah be pleased with her): **"If Muḥammad ﷺ were to have concealed anything that was revealed to him of the Book of Allah, he would have concealed this Ayah."**

**What exactly was concealed?** Tirmidhī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim report, from a narration of ʿAlī ibn Ḥusayn Zayn ul-ʿĀbidīn, that it was the knowledge given him by revelation — that Zayd would divorce her and he would then marry her. This is the view of the majority — Zuhrī, Bakr ibn al-ʿAlāʼ, al-Qushayrī and Qāḍī Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī. Against it stand narrations explaining the concealed thing as love for Zaynab; **of these Ibn Kathīr said, "we did not like to mention these narrations as none of these is sound."**

Zaynab's marriage had a legal objective of Islam to achieve: dispelling, practically and openly, the false notion that marriage to the divorced wife of an adopted son is unlawful. It seems, says Maʿārif, that he ﷺ took the ruling already revealed in 33:4–5 as sufficient, while the need for its practical demonstration escaped his attention — hence *"so that there may be no difficulty to the believers in respect of the wives of their adopted sons when the latter have no desire to keep them."* Ibn Kathīr explains: we permitted you to marry her so that there would be no difficulty for the believers regarding the former wives of their adopted sons — the same exclusion the Qurʼān makes when it forbids "the wives of your sons from your own loins" (4:23).

**"We gave her to you in marriage."** Ibn Kathīr says that the One who was her guardian in this marriage was Allah Himself. Al-Bukhārī records from Anas ibn Mālik that she would say to the other wives of the Prophet ﷺ: **"Your families arranged your marriages, but Allah arranged my marriage from above the seven heavens."** Ayah 37 closes, *"And Allah's command must be fulfilled"* — Ibn Kathīr: what happened was decreed by Allah and was inevitable.

## Ayah 38: no blame, and nothing new

*"There is no blame on the Prophet in that which Allah has made legal for him"* — Ibn Kathīr: in what has been permitted to him and which he was commanded to do, namely this marriage. *"That has been Allah's way with those who have passed away of old"*: **Allah would not command the prophets before him to do anything for which they might be blamed** — a refutation, says Ibn Kathīr, of the hypocrites who imagined there was something wrong in his marrying the former wife of Zayd.

Maʿārif takes the phrase as answering an objection: why such divine concern over this marriage when he ﷺ already had wives? Because this is a *sunnah* of Allah, not something peculiar to Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ: earlier prophets too were permitted plural marriage where beneficial religious considerations called for it — Dāwūd (peace be upon him) had a hundred wives, and Sulaymān (peace be upon him) three hundred. And *"the command of Allah is a decree determined"*: who marries whom is decided by Allah — the mismatch of temperaments, Zayd's displeasure and his resolve to divorce were links in that decreed chain.

## Ayah 39: men who fear no one but Allah

The description in ayah 39 belongs to the prophets just mentioned: *"Those who convey the Message of Allah and fear Him, and fear none save Allah."* Ibn Kathīr: they convey to His creation and fulfil what they were entrusted with, fearing Him and none besides Him, **so no threats on the part of anyone can prevent them from conveying the Message of Allah.**

Foremost in this, Ibn Kathīr adds, is Muḥammad ﷺ: the prophets before him were sent only to their own peoples, while he undertook to convey the message to east and west, to all kinds of the sons of Ādam — *"Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah"* (7:158). Then his ummah inherited the task, the greatest of them his Companions, who transmitted his words and deeds night and day, in private and in public; thereafter each generation inherited from the one before, down to our own time. Ibn Kathīr's closing prayer is worth making one's own: that Allah, the Most Generous Bestower, make us among their heirs.

**A fair objection, answered.** Ayah 39 says prophets fear none but Allah; ayah 37 says to this Prophet ﷺ, "you were fearing people." Maʿārif answers that ayah 39 speaks of fearlessness in *conveying the messages of Allah*, whereas what he ﷺ apprehended was a taunt in a matter that appeared worldly.

## Ayah 40: not a father — but the Seal

*"Muḥammad is not the father of any of your men."* Ibn Kathīr: after this it was not permitted to say "Zayd ibn Muḥammad" — he was not his father, even though he had adopted him.

Maʿārif shows the wording doing extra work: the statement is generalised — he has no son at all. And why "any of your **men**"? Because he ﷺ did have sons — al-Qāsim, aṭ-Ṭayyib and aṭ-Ṭāhir from Khadījah (may Allah be pleased with her), and Ibrāhīm from Māriyah al-Qibṭiyyah — but every one of them died in childhood. Ibn Kathīr notes that he ﷺ also had four daughters from Khadījah — Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthūm and Fāṭimah (may Allah be pleased with them all).

**"…but the Messenger of Allah."** The Arabic *lākin* ("but"), Maʿārif explains, removes a doubt: one might object that every prophet is a father to his ummah, so denying his fatherhood sounds like denying his prophethood. The rules of permissibility in marriage attach to real, biological fatherhood, a different thing from the spiritual fatherhood a prophet has towards his ummah. This also answers the old sneer that he was *abtar*, cut off, with no male offspring to carry his message: that work is done by followers, a prophet's spiritual children.

**Khātam an-nabiyyīn.** Maʿārif notes two recitations of the word — *khātam*, as read by al-Ḥasan and ʿĀṣim, and *khātim*, as read by other leading scholars — with the same meaning either way: the last of the prophets. Why *khātam an-nabiyyīn* rather than "seal of the messengers"? Because by the consensus of scholars *nabī* is the wider term — a prophet may be given a Book and a new Sharīʿah or appointed to guide by an earlier prophet's Sharīʿah, as Hārūn (peace be upon him) was appointed to guide by the Sharīʿah of Mūsā (peace be upon him) — while *rasūl* is used for a prophet given a Book and a new Sharīʿah. Sealing *prophethood* therefore closes the wider door: no prophet of any kind will come after him, with a new law or without one.

Ibn Kathīr states it plainly: this ayah clearly states that there will be no prophet after him, and if there is no prophet after him then there is surely no messenger either, since the station of a messenger is higher — every messenger is a prophet but not the reverse — and this was reported in many *mutawātir* ḥadīths from a group of his Companions. And finality, Maʿārif adds, is itself a mark of excellence: *"Today, I have perfected your religion for you and have completed My blessings upon you"* (5:3).

**From the Sunnah.** Imām Aḥmad records a narration from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"My parable among the Prophets is that of a man who built a house and did a good and complete job, apart from the space of one brick which he did not put in its place. The people started to walk around the building, admiring it and saying, 'If only that brick were put in its place.' Among the Prophets, I am like that brick."** At-Tirmidhī also recorded it and said "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ." As Maʿārif draws the image out: prophethood is a palace built of the prophets, complete but for a single brick, which he ﷺ filled — and even supposing other *kinds* of prophet, there is no space for them in that palace.

Imām Aḥmad also records from Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Messengership and Prophethood have come to an end, and there will be no more Messengers or Prophets."** This worried the people, so he said, **"But there will be al-Mubashshirāt"** — and when they asked what those were, he said, **"The dreams of a Muslim man, and they are one of the parts of prophethood."** At-Tirmidhī also recorded it and said, "Ṣaḥīḥ Gharīb."

**Why this is a red line.** Ibn Kathīr concludes that since there will be no prophet after him, everyone who claims that station after him is a liar and fabricator. So it was with al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī in Yemen and Musaylimah the Liar in al-Yamāmah; and so it is with every false prophet until they end with al-Masīḥ ad-Dajjāl.

Maʿārif records the consensus: all the schools of the ummah are unanimous that there cannot be any kind of prophet or messenger after him ﷺ. The very first general consensus of the Companions formed on this issue, and it was on this basis that jihād was fought against Musaylimah the Liar in the caliphate of Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). Imām Ghazālī, in *al-Iqtiṣād fil Iʿtiqād*, wrote that the whole ummah has unanimously understood from these words that no prophet and no messenger of Allah will ever come after him; Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, in *ash-Shifāʼ*, likewise held that the ummah holds by consensus that this discourse bears its obvious meaning. Maʿārif treats the verse at unusual length because a claimant named Mirzā Qādiyānī invented categories of "shadow" (*ẓillī*) and "incarnate" (*burūzī*) prophethood, which have no proof in Qurʼān or Sunnah at all.

**One clarification.** Finality does not negate the descent of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) in the last days, which Maʿārif says is established from the Qurʼān and from mutawātir ḥadīths, and on which the ummah has consensus. Ibn Kathīr is quoted to the same effect: his being the last of the prophets means the office of prophethood is terminated after him and no one will newly receive it — which does not touch ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), who had already been given prophethood before. When he returns, he will carry out the reform of this ummah in accordance with the teachings of the Prophet ﷺ.

## Living it

Ayah 36 asks us to notice where our own preference is quietly overruling a settled command. The Anṣārī girl in her seclusion and Zaynab bint Jaḥsh both had Sharīʿah-recognised grounds for reluctance, and both let them go the moment they saw where the command lay. And ayah 39 leaves the ummah with the prophets' own work: to convey, and to fear no one but Allah in conveying.

passages.title: Abundant remembrance and Allah's blessings on believers
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move as one passage: a command to the believers, followed immediately by what Allah Himself does for those who obey it. You are told to remember Allah abundantly and to glorify Him morning and evening — and then told that the One asking is Himself sending His *salāh* upon you, that His angels too are asking on your behalf, that He is bringing you out of darkness into light, and that on the Day you meet Him your greeting will be *Salām*. The passage turns from what the servant says to Allah, to what Allah says about and to the servant.

## Where this command falls

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the link with what came just before. The preceding verses mentioned the affair of Sayyidnā Zayd and Sayyidah Zaynab (may Allah be pleased with them), and in connection with it the Prophet ﷺ was declared the last of the prophets — all of it stated in the context of directions for showing him ﷺ respect and reverence, and for saving oneself from causing him any pain. Further on, his perfect attributes are going to be described. His person and his attributes, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, are the greatest blessings Muslims have in this world.

So the command lands in the middle of a discussion of blessings. **The instruction to remember Allah in abundance is given here to show gratitude for those blessings.** Ibn Kathir reads the ayah the same way: Allah commands His believing servants to remember their Lord much — the Lord "Who has bestowed upon them all kinds of blessings and favors" — because this will bring them a great reward and a wonderful destiny.

## The one worship with no ceiling

*Dhikr* — the remembrance of Allah — is what the ayah commands, and it commands not merely remembrance but **"much remembrance."**

The most illuminating comment on this is from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), carried by both our sources. In the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Talhah recorded by Ibn Kathir, he said that Allah did not enjoin any duty upon His servants without setting known limits for it and accepting the excuses of those who have a valid excuse — **apart from *dhikr*.** For *dhikr* Allah has set no limits at all, and no one has any excuse for not remembering Allah unless he is oppressed and forced to neglect it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same statement of Ibn ʿAbbās with the comparison spelled out. Salah is prescribed five times a day, with the number of *rakʿāt* fixed for each. Fasting is fixed to the month of Ramadan. Hajj can be performed only at a particular place and at a particular time. Zakah is prescribed once a year at a particular rate. But *dhikrullāh* is a form of worship with:

- no limit or defined quantity,
- no particular time or period,
- no defined posture or position,
- not even a requirement of purity through ablution.

It is required "all the time, in all circumstances." Ibn ʿAbbās cited the ayah *"Remember Allah standing, sitting down, and lying down on your sides"* (4:103), and the scope is then laid out: by night and by day, on land and on sea, when travelling and when staying home, in richness and in poverty, in sickness and in health, in secret and openly, in all situations and circumstances.

The consequence is exacting, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: in every other form of worship, if one becomes unable through illness or compelling circumstances, one is allowed reduction, brevity, or exemption altogether — but in the case of *dhikrullāh* there are no extenuating circumstances, and no excuse is considered valid for omitting it, except that one may have lost his senses and become unconscious. And the merits, blessings and rewards for doing it are correspondingly numerous.

That is a demand, but it is also a mercy: this is a worship that no condition of your life can lock you out of. Ibn Kathir notes that there are very many ayat, hadiths and reports encouraging the remembrance of Allah, and that people such as An-Nasāʼī and Al-Maʿmarī and others have written whole books about the *adhkār* to be recited at the different times of the night and day.

Ibn ʿAbbās also closes his comment by tying the command straight to the promise that follows it: quoting *"And glorify His praises morning and Asila,"* he says — "If you do this, He and His angels will send blessings upon you."

## What the sources gather here

**"Keep your tongue moist with the remembrance of Allah."** Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin Busr that two bedouins came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. One asked, "Which of the people is best?" He ﷺ said, *"The one whose life is long and whose deeds are good."* The other said: "O Messenger of Allah, the laws of Islam are too much for us. Teach me something that I can adhere to." He ﷺ said, *"Keep your tongue moist with the remembrance of Allah, may He be exalted."* Ibn Kathir notes that At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah recorded the second part of this report, and that At-Tirmidhi said it is *hasan gharīb*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries the same exchange, of a bedouin who said the good deeds and obligations of Islam are many and asked for something concise and comprehensive he could hold on to firmly. Sit with that: a man who feels the religion is beyond his capacity is handed the one practice that fits into any life, in any state, at any moment.

**Better than gold, better than the battlefield.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from Imam Ahmad on the authority of Abū ad-Dardāʼ (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions whether he should tell them of a thing better than all their deeds, most acceptable to their Lord, which would raise their grades, better than giving silver and gold in charity, and better even than going out where you face and kill the enemy and the enemy kills you. When they asked what it was, he ﷺ said: *dhikrullāhi ʿazza wa jall* — the remembrance of Allah, the Mightiest, the Most Glorious.

**Even the Prophet ﷺ asked for it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Imam Ahmad and Tirmidhi that Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said he had heard a supplication from the Prophet ﷺ which he never misses: *"O Allah, make me so that I keep thanking You profusely, I keep obeying Your instructions, I keep remembering You abundantly, and I safeguard Your advice."* Here, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, the Prophet ﷺ is asking Allah for the very ability to engage in abundant *dhikr*. So abundant remembrance is itself something to ask for.

**Past the point of respectability.** Abū Saʿīd (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Remember Allah, the Almighty, so much so that people start calling you crazy."* (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, from Ibn Kathir from Musnad Ahmad.)

**The gathering that becomes a regret.** Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"No people sit together without mentioning Allah, but they will see that as regret on the Day of Resurrection."* A gathering is not faulted here for what was said in it — only for the fact that Allah's name never came up. On that Day the loss will be visible.

## Morning and evening

*"And glorify His praises morning and Asila"* — which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as "in the morning and in the evening," pairing it with *"So glorify Allah when you come up to the evening and when you enter the morning; and His are all the praises and thanks in the heavens and the earth; and in the afternoon and when the day begins to decline"* (30:17–18). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the command as "proclaim His purity at morn and eve."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then offers two readings of why these two ends of the day are named:

1. **"Morning and evening" may, metaphorically, mean all the time** — the two poles standing for the whole span between them.
2. **Or they are mentioned specifically for emphasis** — to stress carrying out *dhikrullāh* at these times and to indicate that it carries more blessings. But that does not confine *dhikr* to them; as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, otherwise *dhikrullāh* is neither specified nor limited to any particular time.

Either way, the two hinges of the day are named, and the whole day is still asked of you.

## He answers your remembrance with His

Now the ground shifts: *"He it is Who sends salāh on you, and His angels too."*

Ibn Kathir reads this as **encouragement to remember Allah: He will remember you, so remember Him.** He connects it to *"Therefore remember Me, I will remember you; and be grateful to Me and never be ungrateful to Me"* (2:151–152). And he reports that the Prophet ﷺ said, conveying what Allah says: *"Whoever remembers Me to himself, I will remember him to Myself; and whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I will remember him in a better gathering."* (Ibn Kathir gives this without naming a collection.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same relation as a sequence: when you have become used to *dhikrullāh* in abundance and have become regular in recounting the perfections of Allah morning and evening, then Allah honours you by bestowing His blessings and by the angels supplicating for you.

### What *salāh* means when the subject is Allah

The word *salāh* here needs care, and the commentators handled it carefully.

On Allah's *salāh* upon the believers, Ibn Kathir reports two positions. **Al-Bukhari recorded from Abū al-ʿĀliyah** that Allah's *salāh* means that **He praises His servant before the angels** — also recorded by Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī from ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas from Anas. **Others said** it means **mercy**. Ibn Kathir declines to force a choice between them: "It may be said that there is no contradiction between these two views. And Allah knows best." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as Allah's bestowing of blessings. Both are affirmed as the sources state them, without likening anything of Allah to His creation and without emptying His words of their meaning.

On the angels' *salāh*: both sources agree it means **their supplication and their seeking forgiveness** for people. Ibn Kathir grounds this in the scene of *"Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify the praises of their Lord, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe: 'Our Lord! You comprehend all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way…'"* (40:7–9). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precision: the single word *salāh* is used in this verse for Allah and for the angels, but the applicable meanings differ — for Allah it means His bestowing of blessings; for the angels, who have no volition of their own, it means their supplication to Allah that He bestow those blessings.

Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) is quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān completing the pattern: *salāh* from Allah is blessing, from the angels it is prayer for forgiveness, and from human beings it is supplication. The one word carries all three meanings.

### Out of darkness into light

*"…that He may bring you out from darkness into the light."* Ibn Kathir ties this purpose back to everything just named: **by means of** His mercy towards you, His praise of you, and the supplication of His angels for you, He brings you forth from the darkness of ignorance and misguidance into the light of guidance and certain faith.

### "And He is Ever Most Merciful to the believers"

Ibn Kathir takes this mercy in both worlds:

- **In this world:** He guides them to the truth of which others are ignorant, and He shows them the path from which others have gone astray — those who call for disbelief and innovation, and their followers among the wrongdoers.
- **In the Hereafter:** He will save them from the greater terror of the Day of Resurrection, and will command His angels to greet them with the glad tidings of Paradise and salvation from the Fire — which, Ibn Kathir stresses, will only be because of His love for them and His kindness towards them.

To convey the scale of that mercy he brings two narrations. Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and a group of his Companions passed by a young child in the road; when his mother saw the crowd, fearing her child would be crushed, she rushed forward crying "My son, my son!" and picked him up. The people said, "O Messenger of Allah, she would never throw her child in the Fire." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said convincingly: *"No — and Allah will not throw His beloved in the Fire."* Ibn Kathir notes that its chain of narrators meets the conditions of the Two Sahihs, although none of the authors of the Six Books recorded it. And in **Sahih Al-Bukhari**, from ʿUmar bin al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him): the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a woman among the prisoners of war picking up her child, clasping him to her breast and nursing him, and said, *"Do you think that this woman would throw her child into the Fire even though she is able to do so?"* They said, "No." He ﷺ said: *"By Allah, Allah is more merciful towards His servants than this woman is to her child."*

## The greeting on the Day of meeting

*"Their greeting on the Day they shall meet Him will be: Salām."*

**Whose greeting?** Ibn Kathir says the apparent meaning — and Allah knows best — is that their greeting comes **from Allah** on the Day they meet Him: He will greet them with *Salām*, as He says elsewhere, *"Salām — a Word from the Lord, Most Merciful"* (36:58). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this ayah as the very explanation of the *salāh* sent to the believers from Allah: on the day they meet Allah, they will be respectfully addressed by Him with *Salām*. **Qatādah** claimed a different meaning — that they would greet one another with *Salām* on the Day when they meet Allah in the Hereafter — which Ibn Kathir likens to *"Their way of request therein will be 'Glory to You, O Allah,' and 'Salām' will be their greetings therein, and the close of their request will be 'All praise is due to Allah, the Lord of all that exists'"* (10:10).

**Which day is "the Day they meet Him"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records three answers. According to Imām Rāghib, it would be the Day of Judgement. Some other leading exegetes say it would be when they enter Paradise, where *salām* reaches them from Allah and from the angels. Yet other scholars consider it to be the day of death, when they leave the whole world to be present before Allah — as Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) stated, that when the Angel of Death goes to a believer to extract the spirit of life out of him, he gives him the message that his Lord has sent him *Salām*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves this generously: the word "meeting" is true in all three cases, so there can be no objection or contradiction in the reports, because *salām* from Allah is sent on all three occasions.

**A ruling drawn from the ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this verse has proved that when Muslims meet each other, their greeting should be *as-salāmu ʿalaykum* — whether from the older to the younger or from the younger to the older. The greeting Allah Himself gives is the greeting believers give one another.

**"And He has prepared for them a generous reward."** Ibn Kathir explains: Paradise and everything in it of food, drink, clothing, dwellings, physical pleasure, luxuries and delightful scenes, such as no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has never entered the mind of man.

## Living it

The passage asks something simple and unrelenting. Since *dhikr* has no fixed quantity, time, posture, or state of purity, the only thing that can keep it out of your day is inattention. So:

- **Attach remembrance to what you already do** — the commute, the queue, the walk, the lying awake. Ibn ʿAbbās's list — travelling and at home, healthy and ill, on land and at sea, by night and by day, in secret and openly — is a checklist of situations in which *dhikr* still applies.
- **Guard the two hinges of the day.** The command names morning and evening; whether as a figure for the whole day or as the hours of greater blessing, they are the natural anchors for a fixed portion of *dhikr*.
- **Do not let a gathering pass without Allah's name in it**, in light of the narration that such a gathering becomes a regret on the Day of Resurrection.
- **Ask for the ability**, as the Prophet ﷺ did in the supplication Abū Hurayrah would not let go of.

And keep the exchange in view. You remember Him; He remembers you. Ibn ʿAbbās's promise sits right at the seam: if you do this, He and His angels will send blessings upon you. He brings you out of darkness into light. And at the end of it, on the Day you meet Him, the word He addresses to you is peace.

passages.title: The Prophet as witness and illuminating lamp
passages.tafsir:
After a long stretch of rulings and social correction, the sūrah turns to address the Prophet ﷺ himself — not with a command first, but with a portrait. Ayat 45–46 name five things Allah made him; ayat 47–48 tell him what to do with them. That is what holds the four ayat together: **identity first, then instruction.** Know who you are, then carry it out — announce good news, ignore the noise, and lean on Allah.

## The five titles

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the text here "reverts to the special perfect attributes of the Holy Prophet ﷺ," and counts five: *shāhid* (witness), *mubashshir* (bearer of good news), *nadhīr* (warner), *dāʿī ilā Allāh* (one who calls to Allah), and *sirāj munīr* (a luminous lamp).

Notice the address itself: not "O Muhammad" but **يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ** — "O Prophet." Allah calls him by his office at the very moment He is describing that office. And notice the verb the titles hang on: **إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ** — "We have sent you." These are not five jobs he took up; they are the shape of a sending.

## Witness — two meanings

**Ibn Kathir** gives *shāhid* two directions at once. He is a witness to Allah's Oneness — that there is no deity except Him — so that his whole life testifies that Allah alone is worshipped. And he is "a witness against mankind for their deeds on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Kathir anchors that second sense in two other ayat: *"and We bring you as a witness against these people"* (4:41), and *"that you be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger be a witness over you"* (2:143).

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** takes the courtroom sense further, citing a hadith narrated by Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and reported by Bukhārī, Nasāʼī and Tirmidhī. In some parts of that narration, on the Day of Judgement Nūḥ (peace be upon him) is brought before Allah and asked whether he conveyed the message to his people. He says he did. His people are brought — and they deny ever receiving anything. Nūḥ is asked for a witness. He answers: *Muhammad and his Ummah.* This Ummah gives evidence in his favour. Nūḥ's people object: how can people who were not even born then testify about us? The Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ answers that no, they were not there — but their Prophet ﷺ told them, and they believe and trust him. And then the Prophet ﷺ himself is asked to testify to the truthfulness of what his Ummah said, and he confirms it.

Sit with the chain in that scene. A community testifies on the strength of what it was told; the one who told them testifies that he told them. Faith in a truthful reporter is itself treated as knowledge worth swearing to.

Maʿārif adds a second, more general sense of his being a witness *for* the Ummah: that he will testify about the good and bad deeds of the individuals of his Ummah. And it gives the basis — that the deeds of the Ummah are presented before him, according to some narrations every morning and evening, according to others once a week, so that he comes to know each individual of his Ummah by their deeds. This is reported from Saʿīd Ibn al-Musayyab through Ibn al-Mubārak, cited via Tafsīr Mazharī. That is a sobering thought to carry into an ordinary day.

## Good news and warning — two audiences, or one?

**Ibn Kathir** reads the pair as pointing outward in two directions: "a bearer of glad tidings to the believers of a great reward, and a warner to the disbelievers of a great punishment."

**Maʿārif** turns both inward on the Ummah: as *mubashshir* he "is the announcer of the good news of Paradise for the righteous people of his Ummah"; as *nadhīr* he "also puts the fear of Allah's punishment in the hearts of his Ummah in case they violate or disobey the injunctions of Sharīʿah."

Both readings are true to the words, and together they are more useful than either alone. Glad tidings are not a blanket reassurance handed to anyone who claims the name, and warning is not something aimed only at outsiders. The believer receives both from the same mouth.

## "By His leave" — the two words that steady a caller

Ayah 46 does not simply say he calls to Allah. It says **وَدَاعِيًا إِلَى اللَّهِ بِإِذْنِهِ** — a caller to Allah *by His leave*.

**Ibn Kathir** unpacks this as: "you call mankind to worship their Lord *because He has commanded you to do so*." The invitation is not a personal project. It is a commission; he is not recruiting for himself.

**Maʿārif** draws out the other half of what *bi-idhnihi* implies: "preaching and inviting towards Allah are very difficult tasks which cannot be performed successfully without Allah's permission and help." So the phrase cuts in two directions — it removes the caller's ego (you were sent, you did not appoint yourself) and it removes the caller's despair (results were never yours to manufacture). Anyone who has tried to speak to a family member about Allah and watched the words bounce off knows both edges of that phrase.

## The luminous lamp

*Sirāj* means a lamp; *munīr* means luminous. This is the fifth attribute, and the commentaries approach it differently — genuinely differently, and both are worth knowing.

**Ibn Kathir** reads it of the message: "the Message that you bring is as clear as the sun shining brightly, and no one can deny it except those who are stubborn." On this reading the lamp is about *evidence*. Light does not argue with you; it simply makes things visible, and a person who still walks into the wall is not confused but obstinate.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reports that "some are of the view that 'luminous lamp' refers here to the Qur'an. But the context suggests that this is also an attribute of the Holy Prophet ﷺ" — since the four titles around it describe him, the fifth most naturally does too.

Maʿārif then quotes **Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh in Tafsīr Mazharī**, who draws a division of labour between the fourth title and the fifth: the Prophet's ﷺ "function of calling towards Allah pertains to his speech and outward acts, his attribute of being a 'luminous lamp' pertains to his blessed heart." Calling is what he *did*; the lamp is what he *was*. "Just as the sun illuminates the whole world, in the same way, the hearts of the faithful become illuminated by the radiant light of his heart." From this Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh concludes that the Companions "are superior and more exalted than the whole of the Ummah, because their hearts were illuminated and graced by his heart directly; the rest of the Ummah received this radiant light indirectly through the noble companions and their successors and so on." Proximity to the lamp is the ranking.

Maʿārif goes on to say that the prophets, and the Prophet ﷺ in particular, are alive in their graves, and that their life in *barzakh* — the state between death and the Resurrection — is far superior to our own life here, its reality known to Allah alone. On that basis the commentary holds that the hearts of Muslims keep receiving light from his blessed heart, each one's share according to the intensity of his love and reverence for the Prophet ﷺ and the abundance of *ṣalāh* (durūd) he sends upon him. This is offered here as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents it — and the guard-rail is the commentary's own: of *barzakh* we say only what Allah has taught, its reality being known to Him alone.

**Why a lamp and not the sun?** Maʿārif asks this directly, since his inner radiance is described there as far brighter than the sun. Two answers are given. First, "the sun illuminates only the surface of the world, whereas his blessed heart illuminates the inside of the whole world and the hearts of the faithful." Second, and more tender: "obtaining advantage from the light of a lamp is voluntary and available all the time easily, whereas approaching the sun is well-nigh impossible and its light is not available all the time." A lamp is in the room with you. You can sit beside it, read by it, carry it. You cannot approach the sun, and it sets. The image is chosen for *nearness and availability*, not for scale.

## Described in the Torah before he came

Both commentaries relay an exchange in which ʿAṭāʼ bin Yasār asked ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ (may Allah be pleased with him) to tell him how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is described in the Tawrāh. They report it separately, with their own attributions and their own wording, so it is worth keeping them apart.

**Ibn Kathir** gives it this way: Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAṭāʼ bin Yasār said he met ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ and asked him, "Tell me about the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Tawrah." He said, "Yes, by Allah, he was described in the Tawrah with some of the qualities with which he was described in the Qur'an: 'O Prophet! Verily, We have sent you as witness, and a bearer of glad tidings, and a warner, a saviour to the illiterate. You are My servant and My Messenger and I have called you Al-Mutawakkil (reliant). You are not harsh or severe, or noisy in the marketplaces. You do not repay evil with evil, but you overlook and forgive. Allah will not take your soul until you make straight those who have deviated and they say *lā ilāha illallāh*, words with which blind eyes, deaf ears and sealed hearts will be opened.'" Ibn Kathir adds that "it was also recorded by Al-Bukhārī in the Books of Business and At-Tafsīr."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** relates the same exchange as reported by Imam Bukhārī, and its rendering of the extract differs in its wording: "O Prophet! We have sent you as a witness, as a bearer of glad tidings, as a warner and as a refuge and protection for the illiterate Arabs. You are My slave and messenger. I have named you 'mutawakkil' (i.e. one who trusts in Allah). You are neither ill-tempered nor hard natured nor one who raises noise in the markets; you do not repay wickedness with wickedness, rather you forbear and forgive. Allah Taʿālā would not recall you from the world till He has straightened out the crooked Ummah through you and they start saying '*lā ilāha illallāh*'. Allah would open up unseeing eyes, un-hearing ears and locked-up hearts through you."

Now read ayah 48 in the light of that. The description says he **does not repay evil with evil, but overlooks and forgives** — and ayah 48 says *overlook their harm*. It says he was **named Al-Mutawakkil**, the one who relies on Allah — and ayah 48 says *put your trust in Allah*. The commands of ayah 48 are not new demands imposed on him; they are the character he was already named for.

Ibn Kathir also cites a long report from **Wahb bin Munabbih** — an account transmitted from earlier scripture, not a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, and to be read as such — in which Allah revealed to the Israelite prophet Shaʿyāʼ (Isaiah) that He would send an unlettered Prophet from among an unlettered people, who "will not be harsh or severe, or noisy in the marketplaces," whose name is Ahmad, and through whom "I will open blind eyes, deaf ears and sealed hearts." The description continues into his Ummah: they will enjoin good and forbid evil, be "like monks by night and like lions by day," their holy Book "in their hearts," and Allah will make them "the heirs of their Prophet, calling people to their Lord, enjoining what is good, forbidding what is evil, establishing regular prayer, paying the Zakāh and fulfilling their promises." The report closes: "This is My bounty which I bestow upon whomsoever I will, and I am the Possessor of great bounty."

That last line lands us straight in ayah 47.

## Ayah 47: the great bounty

**وَبَشِّرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ** — "And give glad tidings to the believers, that they will have from Allah a great bounty."

He was called *mubashshir* in ayah 45; now in ayah 47 he is told, **do it**. The title becomes an imperative. And notice how the bounty is described: not itemised, only sized — *kabīr*, great — with its source named explicitly, **مِّنَ اللَّهِ**, *from Allah*. Maʿārif summarises the instruction as giving "the good news to the faithful that they are going to receive great bounties and mercy from Allah."

The condition attached is a single word: *al-muʼminīn*, the believers.

## Ayah 48: the pressure behind the command

Ayah 48 has four movements: **do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites** — **overlook their harm** — **put your trust in Allah** — **and Allah suffices as a Trustee.**

**Ibn Kathir** on the first: "do not obey them and do not pay attention to what they say." On the second, *wa daʿ adhāhum*: "overlook and ignore them, for their matter rests entirely with Allah and He is sufficient for them (to deal with them)."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** asks the honest question a careful reader will ask: how could the Prophet ﷺ ever be at risk of obeying disbelievers and hypocrites? It answers that it was not possible for him to obey them or to abandon preaching — but that in the situation of this sūrah there was a chance that, in order to avoid people's sarcasm and taunts, he might have inclined to avoid the marriage to Zaynab (may Allah be pleased with her), which was itself a practical demonstration of a divine ruling of the Sharīʿah. *That* is what "obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites" alludes to here.

This is the key that unlocks the passage's placement. The command is not about theological compromise. It is about **letting mockery set your agenda** — trimming an act of obedience because of what people will say. Maʿārif reads the rest of the ayah the same way: he was directed not to mind the vexation he received from them, and not to worry about physical harm from them; and should such a thought cross his mind, to trust in Allah, "because Allah is enough to put all matters right — He will protect him from all harms, and if an apparent harm is caused during preaching, it is a gain in reality, and is not against the promise of protection and putting things right."

That last clause is worth pausing on. Trust in Allah is not a guarantee of a frictionless life. Harm suffered while calling to Allah "is a gain in reality" — the promise is not that nothing will hurt, but that nothing will be lost.

The passage ends on **وَكَفَىٰ بِاللَّهِ وَكِيلًا** — "and sufficient is Allah as a *Wakīl*." A *wakīl* is the one you appoint to handle a matter on your behalf. Having been told not to spend himself answering his critics, he is told who is handling them. Their case is not dropped; it is transferred.

## Living it

Four things this passage asks of anyone who carries any part of the Prophet's ﷺ work:

- **Speak good news and warning together.** Ayah 47 is a command to *tell believers* what Allah has promised them. Encouragement is not softness; it is an instruction.
- **Call by His leave.** Say what you were sent to say, then leave the outcome with Allah — Maʿārif's point that this work cannot succeed "without Allah's permission and help" is as much a relief as a condition.
- **Do not let ridicule redraw your obedience.** That is the concrete meaning Maʿārif gives to "do not obey" in ayah 48.
- **Transfer the case.** *Daʿ adhāhum* — overlook the harm — is only bearable because of what follows it: Allah suffices as the One who handles matters.

And one thing more, from Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh's reading of *sirāj munīr*: the lamp was chosen as the image because a lamp can be sat beside. Increasing your love, reverence and *durūd* upon the Prophet ﷺ is, on that reading, simply moving your chair closer to the light.

passages.title: Marriage law for the believers and for the Prophet
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Ayah 49 gives the whole community a rule about a marriage that ends before it has really begun. Ayat 50–52 then lay out the laws of marriage that belonged to the Prophet ﷺ alone.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the preceding ayah spoke of the Prophet's ﷺ special eminence, and the ayat now coming were to set out the rules of marriage and divorce in which he had a distinction over the general Ummah — but *before* that, a general rule applying to all Muslims is placed as a prologue. Maʿārif counts **seven injunctions** specific to him ﷺ in ayat 50–52; the numbering below follows it.

## Ayah 49: three rulings for everyone

Ibn Kathir opens simply: "This Ayah contains many rulings."

**What *nikāḥ* means here.** Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah uses the word *nikāḥ* for **the marriage contract alone** — you marry, and only then is there anything to divorce — and says there is no ayah in the Qur'an clearer than this on that point. He also draws from it that divorce before consummation is permissible.

**Divorce cannot come before marriage.** Allah says "when you marry believing women, *then* divorce them": contract first, divorce second. Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid bin Al-Musayyib, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, ʿAli bin Al-Husayn Zayn-ul-ʿAbidin and a group of the Salaf took this as proof that a divorce is void if it precedes the marriage. Ibn Abi Hatim records Ibn ʿAbbas saying that if a man declares "every woman I marry is thereby divorced," *this does not mean anything*.

From ʿAmr bin Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"There is no divorce for the son of Adam with regard to that which he does not possess"** — recorded by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah; At-Tirmidhi said, "This is a Hasan Hadith, and it is the best thing that has been narrated on this matter." Ibn Majah also records from ʿAli and Al-Miswar bin Makhramah that he ﷺ said: **"There is no divorce before marriage."**

**No waiting period.** The *ʿiddah* is the interval a divorced woman observes before remarrying. Where there was no consummation there is nothing to wait for, and Ibn Kathir reports the scholars are agreed: she may marry whomever she wishes at once. The one exception, also by consensus, is the widow — four months and ten days, even without consummation.

Maʿārif adds: "touching" means intercourse **actually or by presumption**. If the spouses were alone in genuine privacy, with nothing preventing them and no fear of interruption — *al-khalwah aṣ-ṣaḥīḥah*, "sound seclusion" — that carries the same consequences in law as intercourse. The exemption thus belongs to the woman who went through the nikah and never entered her husband's house.

**Send her away with a gift.** Ibn Kathir says the *mutʿah* intended is more general than half a named dowry or an unnamed gift; both are covered, as at 2:237 and 2:236. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reports Ibn ʿAbbas: if the dowry was named she gets no more than half; if unnamed, he gives her a gift according to his means — **and that is the "handsome manner."**

*Matāʿ* has a wide sense — anything of benefit — so it covers both her **obligatory** right (an unpaid dower, now handed over gladly) and her **non-obligatory** right (clothes at parting, *mustaḥab*, commendable, for every divorced woman). ʿAbd Ibn Humayd narrates the dictum of Sayyidna Hasan that **every** divorced woman is given something as mutʿah — sound seclusion or not, dower fixed or not; and *Badāʾiʿ*, the Hanafi work, even specifies the garments, graded by the families' means.

Ibn Kathir gives the Prophet's ﷺ own example. In Sahih Al-Bukhari, Sahl bin Saʿd and Abu Usayd reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married Umaymah bint Sharahil, and when she came in to him he reached out his hand towards her and it seemed she disliked it — so he told Abu Usayd to give her **two garments**.

**"Release them gracefully."** *Sarriḥūhunna sarāḥan jamīlan.* Maʿārif takes this as the third injunction and says what it forbids: no harsh word **even verbally**, no taunts, no sarcasm. Its larger point is that this law governs how you treat the person you are now **in conflict with**, when emotion is pressing you to take back some of the pain you feel you were dealt. Only the one who governs his own emotions, it concludes, can honour an opponent's rights.

## Ayah 50: the five rulings that were his ﷺ alone

The address changes — *Yā ayyuhan-Nabiyy*, "O Prophet" — and a list follows of what Allah made lawful for him.

**First: his wives**, "to whom you have paid their dues" (*ujūrahunna*, their dowries, as Mujahid and others said). On its face a rule everyone shares; Maʿārif explains the particularity: when this ayah came down he ﷺ had **more than four** wives, and no other Muslim may hold more than four at one time. And the clause about payment is not a condition of lawfulness but a **statement of fact**: he ﷺ paid the dower of every woman he married promptly, in cash, leaving nothing as a debt on himself — recorded so that Muslims will imitate it.

**Second: "those whom your right hand possesses, whom Allah has given to you"** — the captive women who came to him from the war booty, says Ibn Kathir, naming Safiyyah, Juwayriyah, Rayhanah bint Shamʿun An-Nadariyyah, and Mariyah Al-Qibtiyyah, mother of his son Ibrahim. Maʿārif notes that *afāʾa* is from *fayʾ*, technically wealth taken from the enemy **without** fighting, though used broadly here — and cites *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: as no Muslim may marry any of his wives after him, so none may take his bondwomen after him.

**Third: the daughters of his uncles and aunts.** Ibn Kathir notes: "This is justice which avoids going to either extreme." The Christians, he says, would not marry a woman unless there were seven grandfathers between the two, while the Jews allowed a man to marry his brother's or sister's daughter. The pure and perfect Shariʿah cancelled both: cousins permitted, nieces forbidden.

For the Prophet ﷺ a condition was attached: **"who migrated with you."** Maʿārif clarifies this need not mean in his company or at the same time — a woman of his father's or mother's family qualified if she migrated at any time in accordance with his command. Those who did not, did not become lawful for him: Umm Hani', daughter of his paternal uncle Abu Talib, stated herself that she was not lawful for him ﷺ because she had not migrated from Makkah. The condition applied only to his parents' families; for other women, being Muslim was enough. Maʿārif suggests the wisdom: only a woman whose love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ outweighed pride in family would migrate at all.

**Fourth: the woman who offers herself.** Ibn Kathir: she is lawful for him **without a dowry**, if he wishes — the ayah carrying two conditions, that she offer herself and that he wish to marry her. For ordinary Muslims, Maʿārif notes, the dower is so essential that even if bride and groom agree to none, the Shariʿah voids the agreement and the customary dower becomes due anyway.

Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad the incident of Sahl bin Saʿd As-Saʿidi. A woman offered herself to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and stood there a long time; a man then rose and asked to marry her instead. Asked what he could give as dowry, he had only the garment he wore, and could not find even an iron ring. Finally he ﷺ asked whether he knew anything of the Qur'an; the man named some surahs, and he ﷺ said, **"I marry her to you with what you know of the Qur'an."** Also in Al-Bukhari and Muslim, from the hadith of Malik.

Ibn Abi Hatim records from ʿA'ishah that this woman was Khawlah bint Hakim — yet also records Ibn ʿAbbas saying, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not have any wife who offered herself to him." Ibn Kathir explains: he accepted none of them, though they were lawful to him. Maʿārif notes the scholars differed — some say no such marriage is established, others (*Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*) that some are.

**What the community must do instead.** ʿIkrimah — with Mujahid and Ash-Shaʿbi — said "a privilege for you only" means no one else may marry a woman who offers herself without giving her something. Ibn Kathir: on consummation she is owed a dowry befitting a woman of her standing, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ruled for Barwaʿ bint Washiq. Qatadah: no woman may offer herself to any man without a guardian (*walī*) or a dowry — except to the Prophet ﷺ.

**Fifth** — from "a believing woman", Maʿārif derives that unlike ordinary Muslims, who may marry Christian or Jewish women, he ﷺ could not; his wives had to be Muslim.

**"Indeed We know what We have enjoined upon them."** Ubayy bin Kaʿb, Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Jarir explained this as the community's own law — four free wives at most, with walī, dowry and witnesses — *We know it, We legislated it* — "but We have granted an exemption in your case."

**"So that there should be no difficulty on you."** Maʿārif faces the objection: two of these rules clearly ease things, but three **add** conditions and look harder. Its answer: these too were for his good, since without them he would have suffered mental anguish. It also notes a difference over scope — some restrict "a privilege for you only" to the fourth injunction, while Zamakhshari and others apply it to all that precedes. The ayah closes with **Ghafūr, Raḥīm**: Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

## Ayah 51: a concession he never used

**Sixth injunction.** "You can postpone whom you will of them, and you may receive whom you will. And whomsoever you desire of those whom you have set aside, it is no sin on you."

Ibn Kathir reports two readings of *turjī*, which he says means **delay**. On the first, the ayah concerns the women who offered themselves: he may accept whom he wishes and decline whom he wishes, and still return later to any set aside. Its evidence is ʿA'ishah's report (Imam Ahmad, also Al-Bukhari) that she used to feel jealous of those women, and said when this ayah came, "I think that your Lord is hastening to confirm your desire." On the second reading, "whom you will of them" means **his wives**: no sin on him if he does not divide his time equally among them — narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Razin and others, and cited by a group of the Shafiʿi jurists as evidence that equal division was not obligatory upon him ﷺ. Ibn Jarir preferred the view that the ayah is **general**, covering both groups with the choice left to him — "a good opinion which reconciles between the Hadiths," says Ibn Kathir.

**What he did with the concession.** The ordinary rule, says Maʿārif, is that a husband with more than one wife must distribute nights and provision equally; violating it is not permitted. He ﷺ was exempted — and **never availed himself of it in practice.** Al-Bukhari records ʿA'ishah saying that after this ayah he ﷺ still used to ask their permission when changing days, and that she answered, "If it were up to me, I would not give preference to anyone with regard to you, O Messenger of Allah!" Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad that he ﷺ used to divide his time between his wives fairly and treat them equally, then say:

> **"O Allah, I have done as much as I can with regard to what is under my control, so do not blame me for that which is under Your control and not mine."**

Recorded also by the four Sunan compilers; Abu Dawud's report glosses the last phrase as **matters of the heart**, and Ibn Kathir notes its chain is Sahih and all its men reliable. Maʿārif recalls too that in his final illness he sought the permission of all his wives before staying in ʿA'ishah's house, and draws the principle: when Allah granted the prophets a concession, they would generally still act on the original rule out of gratitude, resorting to the concession only at dire need.

**Why this was better for them.** "That is better, that they may be comforted and not grieved, and may all be pleased with what you give them." Ibn Kathir: once they know Allah has declared there is no sin on him either way, whatever sharing he does is his **choice**, not a duty — so they recognise his favour. Maʿārif adds that grievance is born of a due right neglected, whereas a gift from someone who owes us nothing generates sheer pleasure.

**"And Allah knows what is in your hearts."** Ibn Kathir: He knows you are more inclined to some of them than others, which you cannot avoid. Then the names — **ʿAlīm**, All-Knowing of innermost secrets, and **Ḥalīm**, Most Forbearing, meaning He overlooks and forgives. Maʿārif asks why this sentence sits here amid rulings, and cites *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: permission for more than four wives, or marriage without dower, could stir satanic scruples in someone's mind — so the listeners are told to guard their hearts and be firm that these exemptions rest on Allah's wisdom.

## Ayah 52: the wives' reward

**Seventh injunction.** "It is not lawful for you to marry other women after this, nor to change them for other wives even though their beauty attracts you, except those whom your right hand possesses."

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Jarir and others said this ayah came down as a **reward** to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, expressing Allah's pleasure at their decision when he ﷺ gave them the choice: they chose Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the Home of the Hereafter. Their recompense was that Allah restricted him to them — no other marriage, no exchange, however a beauty might attract him. Maʿārif reports the same from Sayyidna Anas: offered worldly comforts with separation from him, or staying with him content with whatever came, they gave up their demand for greater maintenance and elected to remain (Al-Baihaqi, in *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*). Ibn ʿAbbas added the symmetry: as they could marry no one after him, he could marry no one besides them; ʿIkrimah likewise.

**Then Allah lifted it.** Ibn Kathir: the restriction was afterwards lifted and he was permitted to marry other women — **and he married no one else**, so that his favour toward them would be clear. Imam Ahmad records ʿA'ishah saying, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not die until Allah permitted marriage to other women for him"; also in the Sunans of At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i. Read beside ayah 51: twice given a licence, twice he declined it.

**A second reading of "after this."** Others held that *min baʿd* means "after the description We have given" — beyond the categories listed in ayah 50, other kinds of women are not lawful. This was narrated from Ubayy bin Kaʿb, from Mujahid in one report, and others. At-Tirmidhi records Ibn ʿAbbas explaining that Allah made lawful believing women and those who offered themselves, and unlawful every woman following a religion other than Islam — citing "whosoever disbelieves in faith, then fruitless is his work" (5:5). On this reading, Maʿārif notes, the ayah is not a new ruling but draws out the consequence of the previous one; and Maʿārif adds that this second reading finds support in a narration of ʿA'ishah that permission of further marriages remained applicable for him ﷺ. Ibn Jarir held the ayah **general**, covering all the kinds mentioned and the nine wives he had; Ibn Kathir says, "What he said is good," and that there is no contradiction between the two views.

**"Nor to change them for other wives."** On the second reading: even where further marriage remained open under the stated conditions, he could not divorce a wife in order to marry a replacement. On the first, both addition and replacement are forbidden. The exception — "except those whom your right hand possesses" — means, as Maʿārif explains, that a bondwoman he owned falls outside the fifth and seventh rules: she is lawful to him even if Christian or Jewish, and he may replace her with another. The ayah ends with Allah **"Ever a Watcher over all things"** — watchful, says Maʿārif, of the reality of everything, its appearance and its underlying reasons; and so these rulings rest on divine wisdom even where the wisdom is not spelled out.

**On the number of his wives.** Maʿārif answers the usual criticism by chronology: he married Sayyidah Khadijah at twenty-five, an aged widow with children, and spent the whole prime of his life — up to the age of fifty — with her alone, watched by Makkans who called him a magician, a poet, a madman yet never once impugned his purity. And what the later marriages produced was transmission: ʿA'ishah alone narrated two thousand two hundred and ten ahadith, Umm Salamah three hundred and sixty-eight, and more than two hundred Companions learned hadith, fiqh and fatawa from ʿA'ishah.

## Living it

His ﷺ exemptions are not ours to imitate — that is the plain sense of "a privilege for you only, not for the rest of the believers." What the passage puts in our hands is ayah 49: **words bind**, so do not throw conditional oaths at a marriage you have not made; **pay what is owed at once**, as he ﷺ did with every dower, a fact recorded (says Maʿārif) so that we will follow it; and **let go generously and guard your tongue** — half the fixed dower or a gift by your means, with *sarāḥan jamīlan* forbidding the harsh word, the taunt, the parting sarcasm. Beside that stands his own example: released from strict equality, he kept it anyway; permitted more marriages, he took none.

passages.title: Etiquette in the Prophet's homes and the verse of the veil
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take the reader inside the Prophet's ﷺ own household and legislate from what happened there. Ayah 53 — which the commentators simply call **the Ayah of Hijab** — carries three commands: how a guest should behave in another person's home, that the Prophet's ﷺ wives be addressed from behind a screen, and that no one may ever hurt him or marry his wives after him. Ayah 54 seals it with the reminder that Allah knows what you show and what you hide, and ayah 55 names the relatives before whom no screen is required. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: they were first revealed for the Prophet's ﷺ household and his wives, yet — apart from one — they apply to the whole Ummah.

## The wedding feast that occasioned the verse

Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both build the passage on a scene recorded by **Al-Bukhari** from **Anas bin Malik**, who was present at the time.

The Prophet ﷺ had married Zaynab bint Jahsh, and the walīmah was meat and bread. Anas says: "I sent someone to invite people to the feast, and some people came and ate, then left. Then another group came and ate, and left. I invited people until there was no one left to invite. I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I cannot find anyone else to invite.'" The Prophet ﷺ said, *"Take away the food."*

Three men stayed behind, talking in the house. Anas continues: the Prophet ﷺ went out and came to 'A'ishah's apartment and said, *"May peace be upon you, members of the household, and the mercy and blessings of Allah."* She answered, "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah. How did you find your (new) wife, O Messenger of Allah? May Allah bless you." He went round the apartments of all his wives with the same greeting, and each answered as 'A'ishah had. Then he came back — and the three were still sitting and talking. Anas adds: **"The Prophet ﷺ was extremely shy,"** so he went out again. Word reached him that the men had finally left; and as he came back, "when he was standing with one foot over the threshold and the other foot outside, he placed the curtain between me and him, and the Ayah of Hijab was revealed."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds from **the narration in Tirmidhi** that Zaynab was in the room, her face turned towards the wall out of modesty, while the men sat on.

## Other reports of the occasion

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists there is no contradiction between the other accounts: quite possibly all of them together form the cumulative cause of revelation.

- **Sulayman Ibn Arqam, as reported by Ibn Abi Hatim:** the verse came down about some boorish people who would enter a house uninvited and sit waiting for a meal to be cooked.
- **Anas, reported by Imam 'Abd Ibn Humaid:** about people who would find a way into the Prophet's ﷺ house well before mealtime, chat among themselves until the food was ready, and then join the eating. Such things happened before the command of hijab, when men still entered the women's apartments.
- **'Umar bin Al-Khattab.** Recorded from Anas by **Al-Bukhari**: "'Umar said, 'O Messenger of Allah, both righteous and immoral people enter upon you, so why not instruct the Mothers of the believers to observe Hijab?' Then Allah revealed the Ayah of Hijab."

Ibn Kathir places this among the famous cases where revelation confirmed 'Umar's view. In **the Two Sahihs** 'Umar said: "My view coincided with that of my Lord in three things" — his suggestion that Maqam Ibrahim be taken as a place of prayer, after which Allah revealed 2:125; his suggestion that the Prophet's ﷺ wives be screened, since "both righteous and immoral people enter upon your wives," after which the Ayah of Hijab was revealed; and what he said to the wives when they conspired against him out of jealousy, which came down in the words of 66:5. Ibn Kathir notes a report of **Muslim** mentioning the prisoners of Badr as a fourth such matter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to 'Umar's manners: he did not say that his Lord agreed with him, but that *his own opinion* was found to be in consonance with his Lord. That is how a believer reports being right. (On dating: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays that **Hafiz Ibn Hajar in Isabah** and **Ibn ʿAbd-ul-Barr in Istiʿab** report two sayings about Zaynab's marriage — Hijri year 3 or year 5 — and that Ibn Kathir preferred year 5, as did Ibn Saʿd from Anas.)

## Three rules for a guest

**"Do not enter."** Ibn Kathir: believers were forbidden to enter the Messenger's ﷺ houses without permission "as they used to do during the Jahiliyyah and at the beginning of Islam, until Allah showed His jealousy over this Ummah and commanded them to seek permission" — and he calls this **a sign of Allah honouring this Ummah**. He cites the Prophet's ﷺ warning, *"Beware of entering upon women…"*

**"Not so early as to wait for its preparation."** The Arabic is *ghayra nāzirīna ināhu*. **Mujahid, Qatadah and others** explained it as: without waiting for the food to be prepared. Ibn Kathir spells it out: do not watch the food as it cooks to see if it is nearly ready, then come and enter the house. The Arabs had a name for this — **tatfīl**, being an uninvited guest — and Ibn Kathir notes that **Al-Khatib Al-Baghdadi** wrote a whole book condemning it. Come when you are called: *"But when you are invited, enter."* And an invitation is to be honoured — in **Sahih Muslim**, Ibn 'Umar reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"When anyone of you invites his brother, let him respond, whether it is for a wedding or for any other reason."*

**"When you have taken your meal, disperse."** *Fa-intashirū* — scatter, go your ways. And *wa lā musta'nisīna li-hadīth*: do not sit on for a talk. Ibn Kathir: exactly as those three men did, who "forgot themselves to such an extent that this caused inconvenience for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this third rule with its reason attached — the verse itself says such lingering hurts the Prophet ﷺ. So it addresses cases where guests staying on burdens the host: he wants to get busy with his own work, or he has to serve meals to others after them. Where custom is such that guests talking late causes the hosts no difficulty, "this rule would not apply."

## "He is shy of you, but Allah is not shy of the truth"

*Fa-yastahyī minkum* — he is shy of telling you. Ibn Kathir reports the explanation that entering without permission caused the Prophet ﷺ inconvenience and annoyance, "but he did not like to forbid them to do so because he felt too shy, until Allah revealed that this was forbidden." Then *wa-llāhu lā yastahyī min al-haqq* — "and this is why He is forbidding and prohibiting you from doing that."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pulls out what this says about honouring a guest: teaching people how to behave as guests was one of the Prophet's ﷺ own obligations, and still he postponed teaching *his own guests* this etiquette — lest they feel disgraced — until Allah taught it in the Qur'an Himself.

## "Ask them from behind a screen"

*Wa idhā sa'altumūhunna matāʿan fas'alūhunna min warā'i hijāb.* Ibn Kathir: "just as it is forbidden for you to enter upon them, it is forbidden for you to look at them at all. If anyone of you has any need to take anything from them, he should not look at them, but he should ask for whatever he needs from behind a screen."
