Maʿārif ul Qurʼān generalises the rule beyond the household: if non-mahram men must ask women for something of common use, they ask from behind a curtain — speech is permitted through a curtain or something else that obstructs the view.

Anas's report of how the Prophet ﷺ implemented it, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is instructive: when the verse came down he put up a sort of make-shift curtain from a sheet and seated Zaynab hidden behind it — not that he concealed her personally in a burqaʿ or long sheet.

**"That is purer for your hearts and for their hearts."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the most searching point here. On one side, the blessed wives — the very women whose purification Allah Himself undertook, as mentioned in the verse just before this one. On the other, the noble Companions, many of whom have been exalted even above angels. And even between *these* men and *these* women a screen was deemed necessary, for the purity of their hearts and to protect them from sensual scruples. Then comes the question: "Who can claim that his inner-self is purer than those of the noble companions and the inner-selves of his women are purer than those of the blessed wives [may Allah be pleased with them] and thus believe that mixing of men and women would not have any bad consequences?" The command is not a verdict on anyone's character; it is Allah's care for hearts.

## Never to be married after him

*Wa mā kāna lakum an tu'dhū rasūla-llāh…* — the first half, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, declares unlawful every utterance and action that causes the Prophet ﷺ anguish or hurt. The second lays down that no one may marry his wives after him.

Ibn Kathir records from **Ibn Abi Hatim** that **Ibn 'Abbas** said this was revealed concerning a man who wanted to marry one of the Prophet's ﷺ wives after his death; a man asked Sufyan, "Was it 'A'ishah?" He said, "That is what they said." **Muqatil bin Hayyan** and **'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam** said the same, and a chain from **As-Suddi** names Talhah bin 'Ubaydullah, may Allah be pleased with him, as the one who had this intention, until the ayah was revealed forbidding it. Ibn Kathir: "the scholars were unanimous in stating that it was forbidden for anyone to marry any of the women who were married to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the time when he died, because they are his wives in this world and in the Hereafter, and they are the Mothers of the believers."

This is the one ruling in the passage that is *not* general to the Ummah — an ordinary widow may marry another after her ʿiddah expires. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers several reasons scholars have given: they are mothers of the Muslims; the Prophet ﷺ is alive in his honoured grave, his passing being like a husband missing from his home, which is also why his inheritance was not distributed; and, citing **Qurtubi**, that every woman in Paradise would be with her last husband — Sayyidna Hudhayfah told his wife at his death that if she wished to be his wife in Paradise she should not marry anyone after him. So the honour Allah gave the blessed wives in this world was preserved for them in Paradise too. There is consensus in the Ummah that the ruling covers every wife who remained in his marriage until his passing; whether it extends to any who were divorced or who separated for some other reason is disputed, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers the reader to Qurtubi.

*Inna dhālikum kāna ʿinda-llāhi ʿazīmā* — an enormity in the sight of Allah. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah regarded the matter as very serious and issued the sternest of warnings against it.

## Ayah 54 — nothing is hidden

*"Whether you reveal anything or conceal it, verily Allah is Ever All-Knower of everything."* Ibn Kathir: "whatever you conceal in your innermost thoughts, it is not hidden from Him at all," and he brings *Allah knows the fraud of the eyes, and all that the breasts conceal* (40:19) — a verse about the eyes, set beside rulings about looking. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah as guarding the heart: one should not let any doubt or suspicion about these rules enter the mind, and must avoid any violation of them.

## Ayah 55 — those before whom no screen is needed

Allah names those it does not apply to: fathers, sons, brothers, brothers' sons, sisters' sons, their own women, and their female slaves. Ibn Kathir points to the parallel and fuller list in Sūrah An-Nūr (24:31).

One striking omission: uncles. **Ibn Jarir** records that **Ash-Shaʿbi and 'Ikrimah**, asked why the paternal and maternal uncle are not mentioned, answered: "Because they may describe her to their sons, so it is disliked for a woman to remove her covering in front of her paternal uncle or maternal uncle." The concern reaches past the person in the room to where a description of her might travel.

*"Or their own women"* — Ibn Kathir: they do not have to observe hijab in front of other believing women. On *"what their right hands possess,"* **Sa'id bin Al-Musayyib** said this means female slaves only, recorded by **Ibn Abi Hatim**.

The passage then closes: *"And have Taqwa of Allah. Verily, Allah is Ever All-Witness over everything."* Ibn Kathir: fear Him in private and in public, "for He witnesses all things and nothing is hidden from Him, so think of the One Who is always watching." The ayah ends not with further detail but with taqwā — turning the reader back to Allah as *Shahīd*, Witness.

## How the jurists framed hijab

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this ayah as the first verse revealed about hijab, by consensus of the scholars of the Ummah.

**Hijab is not the same as covering the ʿawrah.** Covering the private parts has been obligatory from the very beginning and in the religious code of every prophet — the Qur'an describes Adam and Hawwa' (peace be upon them) patching leaves over themselves (7:22) — and it binds men and women alike, in public and in private. Hijab in the sense under discussion was made obligatory in the fifth year after the Hijrah, applies to women, and applies in the presence of male strangers. Jumbling the two, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns, is where many doubts arise: the face and palms are excluded from ʿawrah under the authority of consensus, so a Salah in which they remain uncovered is valid — but whether they are exempt in hijab before non-mahram men is a separate, disputed question.

**Barring the means.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places these rulings under a broader principle: in the Sharīʿah of Islam not only the sins but even the causes and means that normally lead to them are declared unlawful — as the selling of alcoholic drinks was forbidden along with drinking. Means that generally and necessarily involve one in the sin are unlawful; distant causes are makrūh; causes farther still, involving one only in rare cases, remain permissible.

**Where the scholars differed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out three degrees. The first — that a woman's real place is within her home and she does not go out without need — it draws from this ayah and from the earlier command in this sūrah, *And remain in your homes*, supported by the practice of the blessed wives in **the Sahih of al-Bukhari**: 'A'ishah watching the Prophet's ﷺ grief at the martyrdom of Zayd Ibn Harithah, Jaʿfar and 'Abdullah Ibn Rawahah from inside her room through a crack in the door rather than joining the crowd; and Abu Talhah, when the camel carrying the Prophet ﷺ and Safiyyah stumbled, hiding his own face with a piece of cloth before going to her aid and throwing a sheet over her. It also cites from the **Jami' of Tirmidhi** the hadith of Ibn Masʿud that the Prophet ﷺ said, *"When a woman comes out, the Shaytan marks her out"* — a hadith Tirmidhi termed *hasan sahih gharib*. The second degree is going out, at need, covered from head to feet in a burqaʿ or long sheet, from *they should draw down their shawls over them* (33:59); Ibn 'Abbas, via Ibn Jarir, describes the jilbāb as wrapping her from head to feet with her face and nose hidden too, leaving only one eye uncovered to see the way — with the restrictions that sound hadiths add: no perfume, no ringing ornaments, walking on the side of the street, not entering a crowd of men.

The third degree — whole body covered but face and palms open — is the disputed one, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to attribute the views. It turns on *except that which is apparent* (24:31): some commentators read those words as the face and palms and exempted them (as reported from Ibn 'Abbas), others as the burqaʿ and jilbāb and held exposing face and palms impermissible (as reported from Ibn Masʿūd). Imams Malik, Shafiʿi and Ahmad Ibn Hanbal took the strict position, holding it absolutely impermissible, because it is usually a cause of fitnah even where no fitnah results in a particular case. Imam Abu Hanifah took a different view but conditioned it on there being no apprehension of fitnah — and because that condition remains customarily missing, the later Hanafi jurists ultimately gave the same ruling as the other three; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Fath-ul-Qadir, Sarakhsi's *Mabsut* and 'Allamah Shami in Radd-ul-Muhtar, including Shami's remark that a young woman is prohibited from leaving her face open before non-mahram men "not because the face is included in the 'awrah, but because of the apprehension of fitnah." Certain mahram men are exempted from these injunctions, and very old women are somewhat exempted too.

## Living it

Do not walk into someone's home without permission. Do not manoeuvre for an invitation. When you are invited, come at the time you are called, not before. When the meal is done, read the room and go — the verse's own reason for the rule is that the host may be too shy to tell you.

passages.title: Blessings on the Prophet, curse on his abusers
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In ayah 56 Allah discloses that He Himself, and His angels with Him, send *ṣalāh* upon the Prophet ﷺ — and then commands the believers to join in and to greet him with peace. In ayat 57–58 the reverse conduct is answered: those who set out to wound Allah and His Messenger ﷺ are cursed in this world and the next, and those who wound innocent believers are left carrying slander and open sin.

The verses just before listed distinctions Allah gave the Prophet ﷺ, with the command of *ḥijāb* attached; set in between, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, ayah 56 tells us what those distinctions were instituted *for* — that the greatness of his station be recognised and voiced, and that reverence, love and obedience towards him be absorbed into our own selves.

## Ayah 56: the command Allah performs first

The real purpose of the ayah, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, was to obligate Muslims to send *ṣalāh* and *salām* on the Prophet ﷺ. Allah begins by pointing out that **He** does this, and that His angels do it — and only then are common Muslims ordered to follow suit. Two things follow, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: his station is so high that the act asked of ordinary Muslims is one Allah Himself and His angels already perform; and it proves the great merit of the Muslim who obeys.

## What *ṣalāh* and *salām* actually mean

In Arabic *ṣalāh* carries the senses of **mercy** (*raḥmah*), **supplication** (*duʿāʾ*), and **praise** (*madḥ*, *thanāʾ*) — and which applies depends on who is doing it (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān):

- **From Allah** it means His sending of mercy. Al-Bukhārī reports from Abū al-ʿĀliyah: "Allah's ṣalāh is His praising him before the angels." At-Tirmidhī said this was narrated from Sufyān ath-Thawrī and other scholars: "The ṣalāh of the Lord is mercy."
- **From the angels** it is their supplication for him. Ibn ʿAbbās said, "They send blessings"; in the report from Sufyān and others, the angels' ṣalāh is their seeking forgiveness.
- **From ordinary believers** it is a combination of *duʿāʾ* and *thanāʾ* — asking, and praising.

*Salām* is a verbal noun in the sense of *as-salāmah*, "staying in peace", so *as-salāmu ʿalaik* means: may the state of peace and security from losses, defects and calamities be with you. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a second reading: some other early commentators took *salām* here to mean the sacred Being of Allah, since *as-Salām* is among His beautiful names — on which the sentence would mean that Allah is enough to take care of your security and well-being.

## The honour Allah has already given him

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces what that honour has looked like. **In this world:** his mention was joined to the mention of Allah in the *adhān* and the *iqāmah*; the religion he brought was made to spread and prevail throughout the world; all people were enjoined to keep acting by the Sharīʿah he brought right through to the last day of Qiyāmah, and Allah has undertaken to keep it perennially protected. **In the Hereafter:** his station was made the most exalted of the entire creation, and at a time when no prophet and no angel could dare intercede on anyone's behalf, he was blessed with the celebrated station of intercession called *al-maqām al-maḥmūd*, the Praised Station.

If that honour is Allah's own praise, how can the ḥadīth narrations have *ṣalāh* and *salām* offered to his family and Companions too? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī and others: the degrees of such honour and praise are many. He ﷺ holds it at its highest, while his family, Companions and believers in general are included with him only to a certain degree.

## The Companions asked how — and were taught the words

The ḥadīths commanding this and teaching us how are *mutawātir*, says Ibn Kathīr.

**Al-Bukhārī** records that Kaʿb bin ʿUjrah said it was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, with regard to sending *salām* upon you, we know about this — but how about *ṣalāh*?" He ﷺ said: *"Say: O Allah, send Your ṣalāh upon Muḥammad and upon the family of Muḥammad, as You sent Your ṣalāh upon the family of Ibrāhīm; verily You are the Most Praiseworthy, Most Glorious"* — followed by the same again with *bārik*, "send Your blessings". **Imām Aḥmad** records the same teaching through Ibn Abī Laylā, who said that Kaʿb bin ʿUjrah met him and offered it with the words, "Shall I not give you a gift?" Ibn Kathīr notes that this ḥadīth has been recorded by the Group in their books with different chains of narration.

The wording varies across the reports: al-Bukhārī also has *"…upon Muḥammad, Your servant and Messenger"* from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and Imām Aḥmad *"Muḥammad and his wives and offspring"* from Abū Ḥumayd as-Sāʿidī.

Why did they ask only about the *ṣalāh*? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests they had already been taught the *salām* in the *tashahhud* — *as-salāmu ʿalaika ayyuhan-nabiyyu wa raḥmatullāhi wa barakātuh* — and did not like to determine the precise words of the *ṣalāh* on their own. That is why these words were generally adopted as the *ṣalāh* in the prescribed prayer — though the obligation is not restricted to them, since many different forms of *durūd* have been authentically reported from him ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the exact reported words are certainly far more blessed and bring far more reward.

**Why the method is to ask Allah.** The ayah asks *us* to fulfil his right — yet the method proposed is that we pray to Allah. The hint embedded here, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quoting Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, is that fulfilling his due right of honour and obedience was never within the power and control of any of us; so it was made mandatory that we supplicate before Allah instead.

## What it earns the one who says it

- **Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, At-Tirmidhī and An-Nasāʾī** record from Abū Hurayrah: *"Whoever sends one ṣalāh upon me, Allah will send ten upon him."* (At-Tirmidhī: "This is a Ṣaḥīḥ Ḥasan ḥadīth.")
- **Imām Aḥmad** records from Abū Ṭalḥah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came one day looking happy, and explained that the angel had come to him with news from his Lord: *"No member of your Ummah sends ṣalāh upon you but I send ṣalāh upon him tenfold, and no member of your Ummah sends greetings of salām upon you but I send greetings of salām upon him tenfold."* (Also recorded by An-Nasāʾī.)
- **At-Tirmidhī** records that Ubayy bin Kaʿb asked how much of his prayer should be *ṣalāh* upon him; each time Ubayy offered more — a quarter, a half, two thirds — the answer was *"Whatever you want, but if you increase it, it will be better for you."* Of making his whole prayer ṣalāh upon him, he ﷺ said: *"This would be sufficient to relieve your distress and earn you forgiveness of your sins."* (At-Tirmidhī: "This is a Ḥasan ḥadīth.")
- **Imām Aḥmad** alone records from Abū Hurayrah: *"Send ṣalāh upon me, for this is Zakāh for you; and ask Allah to grant me al-Wasīlah, for it is a position in the highest part of Paradise which only one man will attain, and I hope that I will be the one."*

**The warning against neglecting it.** Imām Aḥmad records from al-Ḥusayn bin ʿAlī: *"The miser is the one in whose presence I am mentioned, then he does not send ṣalāh upon me."* (Also recorded by At-Tirmidhī, who said: "Ḥasan Gharīb, Ṣaḥīḥ.") And At-Tirmidhī records from Abū Hurayrah a ḥadīth naming three men who deserve to be humiliated: the man in whose presence he is mentioned and who does not send ṣalāh upon him; the man who sees Ramaḍān come and go and is not forgiven; and the man whose parents live to old age and who is not granted admittance to Paradise through them. (At-Tirmidhī: "Ḥasan Gharīb.")

## When to say it

**Before you ask for anything.** Faḍālah bin ʿUbayd reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard a man supplicating in his prayer without praising Allah or sending ṣalāh upon the Prophet ﷺ, and said, *"This man is rushing."* Then he taught: *"When any one of you supplicates, let him start by praising and glorifying Allah, may He be exalted, then let him send ṣalāh upon the Prophet, and after that let him make supplication as he wishes."* (Imām Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and At-Tirmidhī reported it and graded it Ṣaḥīḥ; An-Nasāʾī, Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Ḥibbān recorded it in their Ṣaḥīḥs.) At-Tirmidhī records from ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb that a supplication remains suspended between heaven and earth and does not ascend until you send ṣalāh upon your Prophet — narrated also as a saying of the Prophet ﷺ, with the addition: *"Do not treat me like a spare water container — send ṣalāh upon me at the beginning of your supplication, at the end, and in the middle."*

**After the adhān.** Imām Aḥmad records from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ: *"When you hear the Muʾadhdhin, repeat what he says, then send ṣalāh upon me, for whoever sends ṣalāh upon me, Allah will send ṣalāh upon him tenfold. Then ask Allah to grant me al-Wasīlah… Whoever asks Allah for al-Wasīlah for me, it will be permitted for me to intercede for him."* (Also recorded by Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, At-Tirmidhī and An-Nasāʾī.)

**Other occasions** gathered by Ibn Kathīr: entering and leaving the masjid (Imām Aḥmad, from Fāṭimah, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ); the second takbīr of the funeral prayer; the Qunūt of Witr, where An-Nasāʾī's Sunan carries the closing addition *"and may Allah bless Muḥammad"* — and abundantly on Friday and its eve, since (in Imām Aḥmad's report from Aws bin Aws ath-Thaqafī) *"your ṣalāh will be presented to me."* When they asked how, after his body had dispersed into the earth, he ﷺ said: *"Allah has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the Prophets."*

## The rulings the jurists drew

- **In the last sitting of the prayer**, the *durūd* is *Sunnah Muʾakkadah* according to the majority of the Imāms; for Imām ash-Shāfiʿī and Imām Aḥmad bin Ḥanbal it is *wājib*, and if abandoned the prayer must, in their view, be performed again.
- **On saying or hearing his blessed name**, reciting the *durūd* becomes *wājib* — a point of consensus among the majority of Muslim jurists. If his blessed name recurs repeatedly in one sitting, reciting it once may discharge the obligation, but the desirable (*mustaḥabb*) practice is every single time. **In writing** it is likewise *wājib*, and abbreviating it is not enough; write it out in full.
- **Both together are better than one.** Where his blessed name is mentioned, the higher and more desirable choice is that both *ṣalāh* and *salām* be recited and written. Should someone treat one alone as sufficient, it is no sin in the sight of the majority of jurists; Shaykh al-Islām an-Nawawī and others declared it *makrūh*, and Ibn Ḥajar al-Haythamī explained that by *karāhah* they meant *khilāf al-awlā* — contrary to the preferred choice, *makrūh tanzīhī*.
- **The word *ṣalāh* is reserved for prophets** in the view of the majority of scholars. Imām al-Bayhaqī records in his Sunan the fatwā of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Ṣalāh is not sent upon anyone except the Prophet ﷺ, but prayer is made for Muslim men and Muslim women to seek forgiveness for them." For Imām ash-Shāfiʿī, using *ṣalāh* for a non-prophet is perennially *makrūh*, and Imām Abū Ḥanīfah and his pupils hold the same; ʿAllāmah Liqāʾī quotes Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ that major authentic scholars went by this view, among them Imām Mālik, Sufyān and many jurists who held its use for anyone other than a prophet impermissible — comparable to *Subḥānahu wa Taʿālā*, which is particular to Allah. For common Muslims the fitting prayer is for forgiveness and Allah's pleasure, as the Qurʼān has it: *"Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him"* (5:119, 9:100, 98:8).

## Ayat 57–58: the other side of the same coin

**Deliberate, not accidental.** Earlier in the sūrah, Muslims were warned about things that pained the Prophet ﷺ without their meaning it — entering his living quarters uninvited, arriving early for a meal, lingering afterwards in conversation (ayah 53); a warning was considered sufficient. Ayat 57–58 concern pain inflicted *intentionally*, by the disbelievers and hypocrites: the physical injuries done to him on many occasions, and the emotional ones — taunts, insults, false accusations against his blessed wives. Maulānā Ashraf Thānavī accordingly added the word *qaṣdan*, "intentionally", at this place in his summary.

**Can Allah be hurt?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle plainly: Allah is beyond any effect or impression, and no one can cause Him pain in real terms; deeds of the kind that ordinarily cause pain to others have here been *referred to* as causing pain to Allah. On which deeds those are, the leading authorities of tafsīr differ:

- Some maintain these are the specific words and deeds that the ḥadīths declare cause pain to Allah. One is cursing "time". In The Two Sahihs, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Allah says: 'The son of Adam annoys Me by inveighing against time, but I am time, for I cause the alternation of night and day.'"* In the Jāhiliyyah, Ibn Kathīr explains, they would say, "How bad time is, it has done such and such to us!" — attributing the deeds of Allah to time; so He forbade them this. Another such deed, as it appears in ḥadīth narrations, is the making of pictures of living creatures; ʿIkrimah said this ayah was revealed concerning those who make pictures or images.
- Others hold the real purpose here is to warn against causing pain to the Prophet ﷺ, and that it is *termed* causing pain to Allah because that is what it amounts to. This reading is supported by the context, notes Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, since causing him pain is the subject both before and after. It cites the narration of ʿAbdur-Raḥmān Ibn Mughaffal al-Muzanī (Tirmidhī): *"Fear Allah, fear Allah in the matter of my Companions. Do not make them the target of your objections and criticisms… whoever caused pain to them has definitely caused pain to me, and whoever caused pain to me has definitely caused pain to Allah, and whoever caused pain to Allah, it is likely that he will be seized by Him."*

**What occasioned it.** Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the ayah was revealed about those who slandered the Prophet ﷺ over his marriage to Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyay bin Akhṭab. A narration from Ibn ʿAbbās (via Mazharī) ties it instead to the false accusation against ʿĀʾishah: people gathered at the home of the hypocrite ʿAbdullāh Ibn Ubayy to give the slander currency, and the Prophet ﷺ complained before his Companions that the man was causing him pain. Ibn Kathīr and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agree the ayah is general in meaning: it applies to all who caused him pain in any way — that accusation, the taunts thrown by the hypocrites at the marriages of Ṣafiyyah and Zaynab, and the maligning of the other Companions. As Ibn Kathīr puts it, whoever annoys him annoys Allah, just as whoever obeys him obeys Allah.

**A grave ruling.** Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh states in *at-Tafsīr al-Mazharī* that whoever inflicts any pain on the Prophet ﷺ, or suggests any fault in his person or attributes — expressly or by implication — becomes a *kāfir*, and according to ayah 57 the curse of Allah is upon him in this world as well as the Hereafter.

**Why ayah 58 adds a condition.** Ayah 58 extends the protection to ordinary believers, men and women — but with the qualifier *bi-ghayri mā ktasabū*, "without their having done anything to deserve it". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the asymmetry: an ordinary believer may have done something as a consequence of which causing him some pain is permissible under the dictates of the Sharīʿah, so the prohibition is made conditional. With Allah and His Messenger ﷺ it is simply impossible that causing them pain could be justified on any ground — which is why ayah 57 carries no such condition. So from ayah 58 it stands proved: causing pain, harm or hurt to any Muslim without a justification recognised by the Sharīʿah is *ḥarām*.

Ibn Kathīr reads the phrase as meaning they attribute to believers things of which they are innocent. *Buhtān* — the ayah's word for slander — is the most serious kind: telling or transmitting about believing men and women what they have not done, in order to bring shame upon them and accuse them of shortcomings. The description applies above all to those who disbelieve in Allah and His Messengers; then, Ibn Kathīr says, to the Rāfiḍites, who inveigh against the Migrants and Anṣār whom Allah has praised and told us He is pleased with, accusing them of shortcomings of which Allah has stated they are innocent.

## Living it

Ayat 57–58 ask something harder than ayah 56: to guard the tongue. Abū Dāwūd records from Abū Hurayrah that he ﷺ was asked what backbiting (*ghībah*) is, and said, *"It is when you mention something about your brother that he dislikes."* It was asked, "But what if what I say about my brother is true?" He said, *"If it is true, then you have committed ghībah about him; and if it is not true, then you have slandered him."* (At-Tirmidhī: "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ.") Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with the ḥadīth Tirmidhī reports from Abū Hurayrah: *"A Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hands all Muslims remain unharmed and safe; and a believer is the one from whom people remain safe in the matter of their lives and their properties."*

The same mouth is meant for both tasks: sending blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and leaving the honour of Allah's servants alone.

passages.title: The outer garment and the warning to agitators
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Two things that look unrelated sit side by side here: a command about how believing women should cover themselves when they go out (ayah 59), and a blunt threat of expulsion and death against the men who were making Madinah unsafe (ayat 60–62). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows the thread that binds them. The ayat just before this established that causing pain to any Muslim, man or woman, is forbidden and a major sin — and that inflicting pain on the Prophet ﷺ is an act of infidelity, liable to Allah's curse. Ayat 59–62 are the practical follow-through on that principle from both ends: one measure shields the women themselves, the other removes the men doing the harm. Ayah 62 then seals it by naming this as Allah's customary way, which does not change.

## The situation on the streets of Madinah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the occasion in concrete terms. There were vagabonds among the general run of the hypocrites who used to molest bondwomen from Muslim homes when those women came out to take care of family chores. And on occasion these men would mistreat free women too, under the impression that they were bondwomen. So the harm ran in two directions at once, and because of it pain was caused both to the Muslims at large and to the Prophet ﷺ himself.

That is the setting in which Maʿārif reads ayah 59. It is not a discussion of modesty in the abstract; it answers a specific, ugly pattern of harassment, and it answers it in two moves — a change of appearance for the women (59), and a warning of punishment against the men (60–61).

## Ayah 59: the command itself

Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ to command the believing women — especially his wives and his daughters, Ibn Kathir says, because of their position of honour — to draw their *jalābīb* over themselves, so that they would be distinct in their appearance from the women of the Jāhiliyyah and from slave women.

**What is a jilbāb?** Ibn Kathir explains it as a *ridāʾ* — an outer wrapper — worn over the *khimār*, which Maʿārif renders simply as the scarf. He reports this as the view of Ibn Masʿūd, ʿUbaydah, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and others, adding that it is like the *izār* used in his own day — a garment of his time that he does not describe further here. Al-Jawharī is quoted with the plainest definition of all: "The Jilbab is the outer wrapper." So the *jilbāb* is not the headscarf; it is the large sheet thrown on over everything else when a woman leaves the house.

**The wording.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the phrase يُدْنِينَ عَلَيْهِنَّ مِن جَلَابِيبِهِنَّ. *Yudnīna* is derived from *idnāʾ*, which literally means to draw, to pull, or to make come closer. *ʿAlayhinna* means "on" or "over themselves," and Maʿārif glosses it as the sheet hanging as a screen for the face. *Jalābīb* is the plural of *jilbāb*, the name of a particular long sheet. So the force of the command is: take the sheet you already own, and bring it down over yourself.

**How the earliest generations understood it.** Ibn Kathir reports, through ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, that Ibn ʿAbbās said Allah commanded the believing women, when they went out of their houses for some need, to cover their faces from above their heads with the *jilbāb*, leaving only one eye showing — Maʿārif adds the detail that the one eye is left open to see the way. And Muḥammad bin Sīrīn said: "I asked ʿUbaydah As-Salmānī about the ayah *to draw their Jalabib over their bodies* — he covered his face and head, with just his left eye showing." Maʿārif describes the same moment: asked what the verse meant and what sort of covering it required, he answered by demonstrating it — the long sheet pulled from the top of the head and left to hang in front of it, with only his left eye open to see.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this act — the long sheet coming from over the head to hang in front of the face — is precisely the *tafsīr* (explanation) that these authorities gave of the Qur'anic word *ʿalayhinna*. On that basis Maʿārif holds that the ayah commands the hiding of the face with ample clarity, and that this comprehensively supports what Maʿārif itself argued at the earlier verse of hijab: that although the face and the palms of the hands are not included under *satr* as such — that is, they are not part of what must be covered in and of itself — hiding these too becomes necessary under the apprehension of *fitnah*, which is the word Maʿārif uses here for the trouble stirred up by wicked people. Only situations of compulsion stand exempted. That conclusion is Maʿārif's own holding, and it rests on how Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbaydah As-Salmānī understood the phrase *yudnīna ʿalayhinna*.

## "So that they may be known, and not annoyed"

The ayah gives its own reason: ذَٰلِكَ أَدْنَىٰ أَنْ يُعْرَفْنَ فَلَا يُؤْذَيْنَ — "That will be better, that they should be known, so as not to be annoyed." Ibn Kathir's gloss is direct: if they do that, it will be known that they are free, and that they are not servants or whores.

The garment, then, is not presented here as an end in itself but as something recognisable — it reads at a distance, before any words are exchanged, heading the harm off before it can start.

**The obvious difficulty, and Maʿārif's answer.** If free women are told to mark themselves out so that they are not harassed, does that leave bondwomen exposed? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the question head-on. First the legal background: the limits of hijab prescribed for bondwomen were the limits a free woman observes before her *maḥrams* (those marriage with whom is forbidden) — so as leaving the face open before *maḥrams* is permissible for free women, the same was permissible for bondwomen even when they went out, because their very job was to serve their masters, an occupation that took them out of the home repeatedly and made it difficult to keep face and hands hidden. A free woman, by contrast, would go out rarely and for a need, an eventuality in which full hijab should not be difficult. Maʿārif notes that two things were accomplished by the command at once: the women's own hijab came out perfect, and covering the face also distinguished them from bondwomen, so that they automatically became safe from being teased by wicked people.

Then the crucial clarification. Maʿārif insists this never means that Islam allowed a difference between free women and bondwomen in the matter of protecting chastity and honour, protecting free women and leaving bondwomen to fend for themselves. The truth of the matter, Maʿārif says, is that this difference was made by these wicked and low people themselves: they simply did not dare act high-handedly against free women, but chose to tease bondwomen. The Sharīʿah took functional advantage of a difference the harassers had already put into practice, by ordering free women to distinguish themselves, so that the majority of women became automatically protected through their own standing conduct in the matter. The protection of the chastity and honour of bondwomen is as much necessary in Islam as that of free women — but it could not be carried out except by using legal authority. So the next ayah spells out that those who violate the law will not be forgiven: as and where they are found, they will be caught and killed. That, Maʿārif says, is what provided a security shield for the chastity and honour of bondwomen as well.

Maʿārif adds that because the arrangement is complete in this way, the interpretation of this verse offered by ʿAllāmah Ibn Ḥazm and others — which Maʿārif describes as differing from the majority of scholars, and as offered in an effort to escape the very difficulty just discussed — is simply not necessary; a doubt could have arisen only if no arrangement had been made for the protection of bondwomen. That the difference of views existed is itself worth registering: Ibn Ḥazm read the ayah otherwise, and Maʿārif answers him rather than pretending no one differed.

**"And Allah is Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** The ayah closes by naming two of Allah's attributes, and Ibn Kathir ties them to the moment: this is with regard to what happened previously during the days of Jāhiliyyah, when they did not have any knowledge about this. A new command arrives, and it arrives wrapped in forgiveness for the years before it came. The line is drawn going forward, not backward over a past lived without that knowledge.

## Ayat 60–61: the warning to the agitators

Ayah 60 turns to the men, and Ibn Kathir comments on each of the three descriptions it names.

**The hypocrites** — those who make an outward display of faith while concealing their disbelief.

**"Those in whose hearts is a disease."** Here, Ibn Kathir reports, ʿIkrimah and others said that this refers to adulterers in this instance.

**"Those who spread false news among the people in Al-Madinah"** — *al-murjifūn*. Ibn Kathir explains: those who say that the enemy has come and war has started, which is a lie and a fabrication. This is panic-mongering — false alarms of invasion raised in a city where such a claim would land hard. Rumour of that kind is not idle talk; it destabilises a whole population.

The ayah is a conditional: *if they do not stop*. Ibn Kathir marks the condition plainly — unless they give up these actions and return to the truth. The door is deliberately left open. What follows is what happens if they refuse to walk through it.

**"We shall certainly let you overpower them"** — لَنُغْرِيَنَّكَ بِهِم. Ibn Kathir preserves three explanations from the early authorities, each shading the meaning differently. Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah: "We will give you power over them." Qatādah: "We will incite you against them." As-Suddī: "We will inform you about them." Power, incitement, and information — Ibn Kathir sets the three side by side without choosing between them. On the third, what Allah promises His Prophet ﷺ is knowledge of who these men are.

**"Then they will not be able to stay in it as your neighbours but a little while."** "In it," Ibn Kathir notes, means in Al-Madinah. Their tenancy in the Prophet's ﷺ city is on a short lease.

**"Accursed"** — *malʿūnīn*, ayah 61. Ibn Kathir reads this as describing their state while they are in Al-Madinah for that short time, before they are expelled and sent far away. So it is not a label thrown at them in the abstract but a description of how they stand while the clock runs down.

**"They shall be seized wherever found."** Ibn Kathir: they will be attacked, because they are so weak and so few. And وَقُتِّلُوا تَقْتِيلًا — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "killed with a (terrible) slaughter," and by Maʿārif as "killed thoroughly."

## Who exactly is this threat for?

This is the hardest sentence in the passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses it carefully rather than letting it float free.

First, what it is *not*. This punishment is not meant for disbelievers at large. Maʿārif states that numerous textual authorities from the Qur'an and Sunnah bear out that this is not the law of the Sharīʿah of Islam for disbelievers. The law there is that they should first be invited to embrace Islam, along with sincere efforts to remove any doubts they may have. If even then they elect not to enter Islam, they are to be asked to live as *dhimmī* subjects of the Muslim state — and if they accept that, protecting their life, property and honour becomes obligatory on Muslims, very much like that of Muslims themselves. Only those who do not accept this either, and choose the option of fighting, are to be fought back against.

So why is the language of ayah 61 absolute? Because, Maʿārif explains, this matter related to the hypocrites — men who used to call themselves Muslims. When a Muslim starts demonstrating open hostility to and denial of Islam, such a person is called *murtadd*, an apostate, in the terminology of the Sharīʿah. With such a man there is no compromise in the Sharīʿah of Islam, "except that he repents and reverts to Islam and accepts the injunctions of Islam in word and deed." Note that the exception is stated as part of the ruling itself, not as an afterthought: repentance dissolves the whole matter. Otherwise, Maʿārif holds, this person will be killed, as it stands proved from clear statements of the Prophet ﷺ and the collective practice of the noble Companions — citing as sufficient proof the jihād waged against the liar Musaylimah and his cohorts with the collective approval of the Companions, and the consequent killing of Musaylimah.

Two honest notes for the reader. The source drawn on here does not name a hadith collection for those "clear statements," so the teaching is conveyed as Maʿārif conveys it, without attaching it to a named book. And note where the passage locates the acting authority: the ayah's own address is to the Prophet ﷺ — *We shall certainly let you overpower them* — and Maʿārif's whole account of how bondwomen came to be protected turns on the point that this "could not be carried out except by using the legal authority."

## Ayah 62: Allah's unchanging way

سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ فِي الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِنْ قَبْلُ — "That was the way of Allah in the case of those who passed away of old." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: this is how Allah dealt with the hypocrites when they persisted in hypocrisy and disbelief and did not give it up; He incited the believers against them and caused them to prevail over them. And وَلَنْ تَجِدَ لِسُنَّةِ اللَّهِ تَبْدِيلًا — "and you will not find any change in the way of Allah" — means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that the way in which Allah deals with this does not alter or change.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out one implication from this closing ayah: because it cites the matter as the customary law and practice of Allah, it tells us that the punishment of an apostate in the religious laws of the past prophets was no other but killing.

For the believer, this closing ayah also carries consolation. What happened in Madinah was not luck. Ibn Kathir's gloss describes a way of dealing that has run before and does not alter or change: when such men persisted, Allah incited the believers against them and caused them to prevail.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes by drawing two rulings from the passage, and they are worth taking exactly as stated.

**One.** When women have to go out of the house to take care of some need, they should go with the whole body covered with a long sheet, and walk with the face hidden by bringing that sheet from over the head to hang on, or in front of, the face. Maʿārif notes that the common *burqaʿ* also serves the same purpose. Read this alongside the ayah's own stated reason — *that they should be known, so as not to be annoyed* — and the spirit of the ruling is clear: a dignity that announces itself, and is thereby protected.

**Two.** Spreading rumours among Muslims that subject them to anxiety or worry or cause harm is *ḥarām* — forbidden, unlawful. It is easy to file ayah 60 under seventh-century Madinah and move on. But the *murjifūn* were spreading what Ibn Kathir calls a lie and a fabrication — the enemy has come, war has started — and destabilising a community by doing it. That the Qur'an names them in the same breath as the hypocrites and those with disease in their hearts, and warns them of expulsion from the Prophet's ﷺ own city, tells you how seriously Allah treats a tongue that spreads fear.

And running under both rulings is the principle Maʿārif set at the head of the passage: causing pain to any Muslim, man or woman, is forbidden and a major sin. Allah legislated to prevent that harm, He warned those who were causing it, and He forgave what had passed before the knowledge came — *and Allah is Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful*.

passages.title: The Hour and the regret of the misled
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat answer a mocking question with a warning that runs all the way to the Fire. People keep asking the Prophet ﷺ *when* the Hour will come; ayah 63 tells him to hand the question back to Allah — and then, instead of a date, ayat 64–68 give a scene: the disbelievers in the Fire, their faces turned over in it, wishing they had obeyed, and turning on the leaders they followed.

What holds the passage together is that movement from **timing to consequence**. The questioners wanted a calendar. What they are given is the answer to a better question: not *when*, but *what then*. And the last words in the whole sequence are not Allah's but theirs — a supplication, offered too late, asking for punishment on the men they once obeyed.

## The question behind the question

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Those hostile to Allah and the Messenger had just been warned of and alerted to curse and punishment in the present world and in the Hereafter. But many factions among the disbelievers, in their own place, simply denied the eventuality of any Qiyāmah (Doomsday) or Ākhirah (the Hereafter) at all — and because of that denial, they used to ask mockingly: *when* would that Qiyāmah come?

That tells us the tone of the question in ayah 63. "People ask you about the Hour" is not, in this context, the sincere curiosity of a seeker. It is a challenge dressed as an enquiry.

## "Its knowledge is with Allah alone" (ayah 63)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here tells His Messenger ﷺ that **he cannot know** when the Hour will come, and that if people ask him about it, He instructs him to refer the matter to Allah, may He be exalted.

Pause on that. The most honoured of creation, receiving revelation, is told to say: *the knowledge of it is with Allah only.*

Ibn Kathir adds a detail that is easy to skim past. The same instruction was given in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf — **and that was revealed in Makkah, while this sūrah was revealed in Madinah**. Two different places, and the answer has not moved: Allah continues to tell him to refer this matter to the One Who knows about it. But, Ibn Kathir notes, He does tell him that it is at hand.

## Why the Hour is called "near"

Having withheld the date, the ayah presses in the opposite direction: *What do you know? It may be that the Hour is near.* Ibn Kathir gathers the parallel ayat where the Qur'an says the same thing:

- "The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has been cleft asunder." (54:1)
- "Draws near for mankind their reckoning, while they turn away in heedlessness." (21:1)
- "The Event (the Hour) ordained by Allah will come to pass, so seek not to hasten it." (16:1)

Read together, they say more than "one day it will happen." The Hour has *already* drawn near (54:1); people turn away in heedlessness precisely while their reckoning approaches (21:1); and what is ordained will come to pass, so it is not to be hastened (16:1).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons the Hour is described as near:

**First, because nobody knows its exact date** — and therefore everyone should be prepared for it as if it were very close. That is the instruction the passage leaves us with in place of a date.

**Second, because of how it will feel from the other side.** After facing the horrible incidents of Qiyāmah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the entire worldly life — even thousands of years of it — will seem to be very short, and the Qiyāmah very close to it. "Near" is not only a statement about the calendar; it is a statement about proportion.

## The curse, the Fire, and "forever" (ayat 64–65)

Now the answer turns from timing to outcome, and each phrase closes a door.

**"Verily, Allah has cursed the disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is worth memorising. It means: **He has distanced them from His mercy.** That is the essence of the divine curse — not that something was hurled at them, but that the one thing every creature depends on has been put out of reach. Everything that follows in these ayat is what existence looks like once mercy is at that distance.

**"and has prepared for them a flaming Fire."** Ibn Kathir notes simply: this means, in the Hereafter.

**"Wherein they will abide forever."** Ibn Kathir spells out the force of it: they will stay there **forever and ever, never leaving or finding relief from it**. Not only no exit — no let-up either.

**"and they will find neither a protector nor a helper."** Ibn Kathir: they will have no saviour to help them or rescue them from their predicament.

Notice the order of the passage. Ayah 65 has already ruled out any protector and any helper *before* the chiefs and great ones are so much as mentioned. So when the followers begin appealing about those leaders in ayat 67–68, the text has already told us what such an appeal can achieve.

## Faces turned over in the Fire (ayah 66)

"On the Day when their faces will be turned over in the Fire, they will say: 'Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger.'" Ibn Kathir describes what this means: they will be dragged into the Fire on their faces, and their faces will be contorted in Hell — and in that state they will wish that they had been among those who had obeyed Allah and His Messenger ﷺ in this world.

Their words are pure longing: *would that we had…* — a wish for something that can no longer be had.

Ibn Kathir places this cry alongside its sisters in the Qur'an. From Sūrat al-Furqān: "And the Day when the wrongdoer will bite at his hands, he will say: 'Oh! Would that I had taken a path with the Messenger. Ah! Woe to me! Would that I had never taken so-and-so as an intimate friend! He indeed led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me. And Shayṭān is to man ever a deserter in the hour of need.'" (25:27–29) And: "How much would those who disbelieved wish that they had been Muslims." (15:2)

Set those next to our passage and a pattern emerges. The regret described is regret over **companionship and following** — the intimate friend, the one who led them astray. And the one who leads astray abandons them: "Shayṭān is to man ever a deserter in the hour of need."

## One verb, two masters (ayat 66–67)

This is the hinge of the passage, and it turns on a single Arabic word used twice.

In ayah 66: *aṭaʿnā-llāha wa aṭaʿnā-r-rasūl* — "would that we had **obeyed** Allah and **obeyed** the Messenger."

In ayah 67: *innā aṭaʿnā sādatanā wa kubarāʼanā* — "verily, we **obeyed** our chiefs and our great ones."

The same verb, *aṭāʿa*, to obey. Nobody in these ayat failed to obey; the difference is *whose* obedience it was. What they wish for in ayah 66 is not that they had obeyed nothing, but that they had obeyed Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

Note also the two objects in ayah 66: obedience to Allah **and** obedience to the Messenger ﷺ, named separately. The very thing they would not do in life is the thing they name in their regret.

## "Our chiefs and our great ones" (ayah 67)

Who are these figures? Ibn Kathir preserves the explanation of the early authority **Ṭāwūs**: "'our chiefs' means their **nobles**, and 'our great ones' means their **scholars**."

That reading puts two very different kinds of authority side by side — rank and standing on one hand, learning on the other. And here both are named by their own followers as the reason they are in the Fire: "and they misled us from the way."

Two things must be held together, and the passage supports both. The followers do not escape: they are the ones in the Fire saying these words, and ayah 65 has already ruled out any protector or helper for them. And yet misleading others is itself charged — the next ayah is about exactly that.

## The last supplication of the misled (ayah 68)

Their final words are a plea: "Our Lord! Give them **double** torment and curse them with a mighty curse!"

Ibn Kathir explains the doubling: it is **"for their disbelief and because they mislead us"** — two counts, therefore two shares.

And look where the word for cursing has travelled. Ayah 64 opened with Allah having cursed the disbelievers — distancing them from His mercy. Ayah 68 closes with those same people begging Allah to curse their chiefs "with a mighty curse". In between, the ones who said "we obeyed our chiefs and our great ones" have become the ones asking for those chiefs' torment to be doubled. What was obedience in this world ends as accusation.

There is something almost unbearable about the shape of it: their last recorded speech is not a request for their own rescue, but a plea for someone else's ruin.

## These ayat used as a warning

Ibn Kathir relates a report showing these ayat put to use as a warning among Muslims. **Abū al-Qāsim aṭ-Ṭabarānī recorded from Abū Rāfiʿ** that among the names of those who fought with ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, was al-Ḥajjāj bin ʿAmr bin Ghaziyah — and he was the one who, when they met, said: *"O people of the Anṣār! Do you want to say when we meet our Lord: 'Our Lord! Verily, we obeyed our chiefs and our great ones, and they misled us from the way. Our Lord! Give them double torment and curse them with a mighty curse!'?"*

He was using these very ayat as a question put to men about to act: *is this the speech you are preparing for yourself?* Not as history about ancient disbelievers, but as a mirror held up to those choosing whom to follow.

## Living it

**Stop asking when; start asking whether you are ready.** The passage refuses the date and supplies the preparation instead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws exactly this conclusion: since nobody knows the exact date, everyone should be prepared for it as if it were very close.

**Audit your obedience, not just your beliefs.** These ayat do not describe people who obeyed nothing. They describe people who obeyed their chiefs and their great ones — as Ṭāwūs read it, their nobles and their scholars. Ask of any authority you follow: does this lead me toward obeying Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, or away from it? Ayah 66 tells you which obedience you will wish you had chosen.

**"He led me astray" is not a way out.** They say it from inside the Fire, and they are still in it — ayah 65 has already said they will find no protector and no helper.

**If people follow you, take that seriously.** A parent, a teacher, an older sibling, anyone others listen to: the doubled torment in ayah 68 is, as Ibn Kathir explains it, for disbelief *and* for misleading. Influence is not weightless.

**And measure this life by the scale Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers.** Whatever length it feels like from inside, after the events of Qiyāmah even thousands of years of it will seem very short. Everything in the passage that sounds severe — the curse, the Fire, the forever, the absence of any protector — is being told to us now, before that Day. The people in ayat 66–68 are given words of regret they can no longer use. We have been shown those words while we can still make them unnecessary.

passages.title: Do not slander as Moses was slandered
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take the warning of the previous verse — that causing pain to Allah and His Messenger brings fatal consequences — and turn it into a practical programme for the believing community. Ayah 69 holds up a mirror from history: a prophet wounded by the tongues of his own people. Ayat 70–71 then hand us the cure: guard your speech, and Allah will put the rest of your life right. What binds the passage together is the tongue — first as the instrument that injures a prophet, then as the instrument that, once disciplined, becomes the key to a whole righteous life.

*A note on how this is written: passages of tafsir are attributed to the commentary they come from — Ibn Kathir or Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. Paragraphs set off as blockquotes and marked "Reflection" are not tafsir; they are this writer's own devotional response, offered as such.*

## The warning by way of a mirror

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the flow carefully. The verse before spoke of the fatal consequences of hurting Allah and His Messenger; ayah 69 now instructs the believers to guard particularly against falling into any stance of hostility toward Allah and His Messenger, because such a stance causes pain.

And it does this in a striking way: instead of accusing anyone, it points to another people and another prophet. **"O you who believe! Be not like those who annoyed Musa."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an important point here — it does not necessarily follow from this that the Muslims had actually done such a thing. The incident is related as a forewarning, a matter of precaution. Whatever incidents of intentionally causing pain there are, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, they all relate to the hypocrites. That a Companion would intentionally cause the Holy Prophet ﷺ pain is not possible; as for the incident of some Companions reported in a narration, it is likely they did not realise at the time that the word being said would cause him pain.

So the mirror is held up as precaution, not accusation.

> **Reflection.** There is a mercy in being taught this way — shown someone else's failure before we have committed it ourselves, and warned off it while there is still nothing to confess.

## The story the Prophet ﷺ told about Musa

What exactly did the Children of Israel do to Musa? Remarkably, we are not left to guess: the Prophet ﷺ explained this very ayah himself. Ibn Kathir records that Al-Bukhari reported it in the Book of Hadiths about the Prophets — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Imam al-Bukhari reported it from Abu Hurayrah in Kitab al-Tafsir and Kitab al-Anbiya'. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Musa, peace be upon him, was a shy and modest man who would never show anything of his skin, out of his shyness.

Some of the Children of Israel annoyed him over it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the cultural texture: among Bani Isra'il men would commonly bathe naked before everybody, while Musa would take his bath inside a screened place, and no one had the occasion to see his body uncovered. So some of them began to say: *he only keeps himself covered because of some defect in his skin — either leprosy, or scrotal hernia, or some other defect.*

Then Allah, may He be glorified, willed to clear Musa of what they were saying. One day Musa was alone; he took off his garment and put it on a rock, then bathed. When he had finished and turned back to pick up his garment, the rock moved away, taking the garment with it. Musa picked up his stick and chased the rock, saying, *"My garment, O rock! My garment, O rock!"* — until he reached a group of the Children of Israel. They saw him uncovered and found that he was **the best of those whom Allah had created**; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that they saw a body that was perfect, without the defect they had attributed to him. Thus he was cleared of what they had said about him. Then the rock stood still, and he took his garment and put it on. He began hitting the rock with his stick, and — *"by Allah,"* said the Prophet ﷺ — the marks of that beating were left on the rock, three or four or five. And then he said: this is what is referred to in the ayah, *"O you who believe! Be not like those who annoyed Musa, but Allah cleared him of that which they alleged, and he was honorable before Allah."* Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith is one of those recorded by Al-Bukhari but not Muslim.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws a point here about weighing reports. The explanation of the pain caused to Musa in this incident has been reported from the Holy Prophet ﷺ himself. There is another story relating to the pain caused to him reported from the noble Companions, which is also appended to it — but, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, *the weightier explanation is the one that is present in the hadith reported from the Holy Prophet ﷺ himself.*

> **Reflection.** What strikes me most is how ordinary the sin is. A rumour about a man's body, born from finding his modesty strange. No violence, no plot — just talk. And yet this is the incident the ayah preserves as the pattern of injuring a prophet.

## Why Allah went to such lengths

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reflects on the sheer scale of Allah's intervention: in this event Allah demonstrated such unusual concern to have Musa absolved of the blame imputed to him that it took no less than a miracle — a rock running away with his clothes, so that he was compelled by circumstances beyond his control to come out uncovered before the people.

This extraordinary care, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues, points to a general reality: Allah keeps even the bodies of His prophets generally free and pure of defects that appear repulsive and undignified — as stands proved from the hadith of Bukhari that all prophets are lineally high-born. The reason given is practical: it would be hard to agree to listen to, accept and follow someone from a line and family that people customarily regard as low. Similarly, the history of the prophets does not bear out that any prophet was blind, deaf, dumb or handicapped. And what of Ayyub, peace be upon him? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that his case cannot be used to raise an objection: what happened to him was the dictate of divine wisdom — a particular trial, a temporary discomfort, eliminated later on. **And Allah knows best.**

> **Reflection.** There is consolation here for anyone who has been talked about unjustly. Allah defended Musa's dignity publicly, at His own chosen moment, in a way no human effort could have arranged.

## "And he was honourable before Allah"

The ayah closes on Musa's standing: *wa kāna ʿinda Allāhi wajīhan.* Ibn Kathir explains this to mean he had a position of status and honour before his Lord, may He be exalted and glorified. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up: **wajīh** denotes the honour and elegance of someone who deserves regard and consideration. Used together with *ʿinda Allāh* ("in the sight of Allah"), it would mean a person whose prayer Allah answers and whose wish He does not turn down.

Al-Hasan Al-Basri put it exactly so: **"His supplications would be answered by Allah."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Musa's station as one whose prayers were answered — popularly known as *mustajāb al-daʿawāt* — is proved from many events mentioned in the Qur'an where he prayed to Allah for something and He answered it the way he wanted it to be.

Both commentaries single out the same example. Ibn Kathir reports that some of them said part of Musa's great standing before Allah was that he interceded for his brother Harun, asking Allah to send him with him as a Messenger — and Allah granted his request: *"And We granted him his brother Harun, (also) a Prophet, out of Our mercy"* (19:53). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the most unique of his answered prayers, and closes the discussion — crediting Ibn Kathir — with the observation that the high office of prophethood is not given to someone on someone's recommendation. That Allah nonetheless answered this request is the measure of how *wajīh* Musa was with Him.

## "May Allah have mercy on Musa"

Ibn Kathir gives an incident that shows the Prophet ﷺ himself bearing such hurt. Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud said: one day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ distributed some booty, and a man among the Ansar said, *"This division was not done for the sake of Allah."* Ibn Masʿud said, "O enemy of Allah! I am going to tell the Messenger of Allah ﷺ what you have said." So he told the Prophet ﷺ about it. His face reddened, and he said: **"May Allah have mercy on Musa. He was annoyed with worse than this, yet he remained patient."** Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded in the Two Sahihs.

> **Reflection.** The reddened face tells us the hurt was real. And still the response was not self-defence but the remembrance of a brother prophet who bore worse and stayed patient — the ayah working in both directions at once: a warning about our own tongues, and a comfort for anyone wounded by someone else's.

## Ayah 70: taqwa, and then one concrete thing

**"O you who believe! Have Taqwa of Allah and speak (always) the truth."**

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here commands His servants to have taqwa of Him — *worshipping Him as if they can see Him* — and to speak *qawlan sadīdan*, meaning to speak in a straightforward manner, with no crookedness or distortion.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks why the command comes in this order. The reality of taqwa lies in total obedience to all divine injunctions, carrying out everything enjoined and abstaining from everything declared prohibited and repugnant. And it is obvious that doing so is no easy task for human beings. Therefore, immediately after the main guideline *ittaqū Allāh*, there appears an instruction to start doing something particular: the correction and reform of one's speech. This too is nothing but a part of taqwa itself — yet it is one such part that, should it come under control, all the other remaining components of taqwa would start becoming achievable, as the verse itself promises.

## The word *sadīd*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the linguistic heart of the passage. Some exegetes explained *sadīd* as what is the truth; others as straight; still others as correct. Quoting all of these, Ibn Kathir calls all of them true — the sense being that of hitting the target.

And this is why, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the Qur'an chose this word instead of *ṣādiq* ("truthful") or *mustaqīm* ("straight"): the present word holds all these attributes of ideal speech within itself. It was for this reason that Kashifi said in *Ruh-ul-Bayan* that *qawl sadīd* is:

- the saying of what is **true**, having no trace of falsity;
- **correct**, having no trace of error;
- the **right** thing, being no joke or fun;
- **spoken softly**, not harshly.

> **Reflection.** Notice how much wider this is than "don't lie." Two of the four marks are not about truth at all, but about manner: whether the words are made sport of, and how gently they are said.

## Ayah 71: the tongue as the master key

**"He will bless your deeds for you, and forgive your sins."**

Ibn Kathir explains the promise: if they do that, Allah will reward them by making their deeds righteous — that is, enabling them to do righteous deeds — and He will forgive them their past sins. As for whatever sins they may commit in the future, He will inspire them to repent from them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the mechanism in a memorable way: correct use of one's power of speech is an effective source of correcting all the deeds issuing forth from the other parts of the body. In other words: *should you succeed in holding your tongue and avoiding errors of speech and get used to saying what is correct, straight and right, Allah will correct every other deed you do and make all of them better.* One who gains control over his tongue and becomes used to saying what is true and right will find that Allah takes care of the rest of his deeds, has them corrected and made better, and forgives any errors or slips made therein.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Shah ʿAbdul-Qadir of Delhi translated the ayah in a way that leads to the conclusion that this promise is not restricted to religious deeds alone: everything one does in this material world is included too. Anyone who gets used to saying the right thing — never lying, speaking with deliberation without erring or wavering, not deceiving anyone, not saying what would hurt — shall find his deeds for the eternal life of the Hereafter coming out right for him, and the things he must do to live in this mortal world turning for the better as well.

## A pattern worth noticing: the Qur'an makes taqwa easy

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a broader observation from deliberating on the general style of the Qur'an: where acting on an injunction seems difficult, a method has also been suggested along with it to make it easy. And since taqwa is the essence of the entire religion and fulfilling its dictates on all counts is very hard indeed, generally speaking, wherever the command *ittaqū Allāh* has been given, there appears soon after a suggestion of something that facilitates acting in accordance with the rest of the elements of taqwa — something that comes from the side of Allah as His grace and enabling (*tawfīq*).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this very passage the apt and ready-to-hand example: *"say the right thing"* follows soon after *"fear Allah."* And the warning about Musa, it says, works the same way, by clearing an obstacle: people were reminded that causing pain to the righteous and favoured servants of Allah is the most serious impediment to the achievement of taqwa, and once this impediment is removed the way to taqwa becomes easy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to two parallels elsewhere. In another verse the command of taqwa is supplemented by the direction of having the company of the truthful (9:118) — meaning the easiest way to acquire taqwa is to remain in the company of righteous people. At another place the command of taqwa is followed by the direction of pondering what one has sent ahead for the Hereafter (59:18), because that leads one to observe taqwa.

## "A great victory"

**"And whosoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, he has indeed achieved a great victory."**

Ibn Kathir explains the *fawz ʿaẓīm* concretely: he will be saved from the fire of Hell and will enjoy everlasting delights in Paradise.

## Living it — a closing reflection

*What follows is application rather than commentary: how these three ayat might land on an ordinary day.*

**Do not be a person whose talk wounds the righteous.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names causing pain to the righteous and favoured servants of Allah as the most serious impediment to attaining taqwa. That is a striking place to locate an obstacle — not in some grand sin, but in talk.

**Start your taqwa at your tongue.** Of all the fronts on which taqwa must be fought, ayah 70 names this one, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why: bring this part under control and the other parts begin to become achievable.

**Aim at all four marks of *sadīd*.** True, correct, not made a joke of, and softly spoken. Most of us are content with the first.

**Trust Allah with your reputation.** Musa was cleared by Allah, publicly and beyond anyone's engineering, and his standing — *wajīh ʿinda Allāh* — was never in the hands of those who talked about him.
