These two ayat close Sūrah al-Aḥzāb by naming what human beings are actually carrying: a **trust** so heavy that the heavens, the earth and the mountains declined it, and man accepted it. Ayah 72 tells the offer; ayah 73 the outcome. Because man took the trust on, reward and punishment became real for him.

**Where this comes in the sūrah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the whole of al-Aḥzāb has pressed one theme: reverence for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the obligation of obeying him. Now the great station and *rank* of that obedience is disclosed. Obedience to Allah and His Messenger, and the carrying out of their commands, is given a name — *amānah*, trust.

## What is the "amānah"?

The Companions and the early scholars answered this in several ways, and Ibn Kathir gathers them:

- **Obedience.** Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that al-amānah means obedience, offered to the heavens, earth and mountains before it was offered to Adam (peace be upon him).
- **Al-Farāʼiḍ — the obligatory duties.** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported this from Ibn ʿAbbās, and it was also the view of Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.
- **Chastity.** Al-Aʿmash narrated from Abū aḍ-Ḍuḥā from Masrūq that Ubayy bin Kaʿb said: part of al-amānah is that woman was entrusted with her own chastity.
- **Religion, obligatory duties and prescribed punishments** — Qatādah.
- **Prayer, fasting, and performing ghusl (the purifying bath) to cleanse oneself from sexual impurity** — Zayd bin Aslam, narrated by Mālik.

Ibn Kathir's verdict: "There is no contradiction between all of these views; they are all in agreement." Each names a specimen of one thing — **responsibility: the acceptance of commands and prohibitions with their attendant conditions** — whoever fulfils this responsibility is rewarded and whoever neglects it is punished.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same conclusion from Qurṭubī — the majority of commentators hold that *all* areas of religious conduct are included — and from Tafsīr Mazharī, that the whole package of obligations and prohibitions set by the Sharīʿah is amānah. Abū Ḥayyān put it most sweepingly in *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*: apparently it is everything one is entrusted with, of command and prohibition, and every state of life relating to this world or the Hereafter — in fact the Sharīʿah, all of it, is amānah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up: amānah means to be obligated with the precepts and injunctions of the Sharīʿah and to be under command to carry them out — with the eternal blessings of Jannah promised once this is accomplished to the best of one's ability, and the punishment of Jahannam for contravention or shortcoming.

## A second sense: the *capacity* to carry it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further layer from some early commentators. The amānah can also refer to **the capability of fulfilling the heavy responsibility placed by divine injunctions** — something that depends on a particular degree of reason and awareness. Moving forward therein, and deserving the office of divine vicegerency, depends on this very capability.

The skies, the earth, even the angels have no inherent ability to go forward from where they are; everything among these creatures is restricted to whatever station of nearness to its Creator it already holds: *"There is no one among us who does not have a known station"* (aṣ-Ṣāffāt 37:164). Man alone was given a station that can be climbed — and, therefore, fallen from.

## Did this offer really happen?

The verse says Allah *offered* the amānah to the heavens, the earth and the mountains. But these are, to all appearances, inanimate and devoid of knowledge and consciousness: how then can an offer be made to them, and how can they answer?

**Some early commentators** took this to be a figure of speech, comparing it to another verse: *"Had We sent down this Qurʼān to a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, burst apart out of awe for Allah"* (al-Ḥashr 59:21) — an example given as a matter of supposition.

**But in the sight of the majority of Muslim scholars**, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that reading is not correct here, on two grounds:

1. **Grammar.** The verse of al-Ḥashr opens with *"Had We…"* — the Qurʼān itself makes clear it is hypothetical. Ayah 72 is not framed that way; it is the affirmation of an incident in a descriptive style. And it is not permissible to take it in a figurative or metaphorical sense without any proof.
2. **The Qurʼān's own testimony about creation.** *"And there is not a single thing that does not extol His purity and praise"* (al-Isrāʼ 17:44). To know Allah, to realise that He is the Creator, the Master, the highest and the best, and to glorify Him accordingly, is not possible without knowledge and consciousness. So knowledge and consciousness exist throughout creation, even in what is considered inanimate — enough that these things can be addressed and a response expected from them.

It is not rationally impossible that Allah could bestow on the heavens, the earth and the mountains the functional ability to verbalise and speak. Hence, in the sight of the majority of the learned among this Ummah, the offering of the trust came to pass in reality, and their expression of inability was in reality too.

## Why were they able to refuse?

When Allah Himself made the offer of this great trust, how could any creature dare refuse it? Elsewhere the heavens and earth are shown as perfectly compliant: *"we come in obedience"* (Fuṣṣilat 41:11).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers by the difference between a command and an offer. In 41:11 the address carried a **mandatory command** — willingly or unwillingly, they had to obey; and they responded that they were pleased to come. Ayah 72 is different: **they were given the choice**.

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, is emphatic: "they did not want to do that, and they were afraid of it, **not because their intention was sinful, but because of their respect for the religion of Allah**, in case they could not fulfil the obligations involved." Their refusal was reverence, not rebellion.

## The scene itself

Ibn Kathir, with the support of various authorities, reports from several Companions and Successors — Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Mujāhid and others — the details of this offer. It went first to the heavens, then the earth, then the mountains, as a matter of choice: *would you undertake to carry out the responsibility imposed by this trust, against a return fixed for it?* Each asked what the return was. The answer: if you fulfil its demands to the best of your ability, you will have the best of reward, and particularly the honour of nearness to Allah; and if you fail to implement these injunctions, or fall short, you will be punished. At that, all these huge bodies responded: *O our Lord, we are operating under Your command even now. But now that we have been given a choice, we find ourselves weak and unable to bear the burden of this heavy responsibility. As reward, we do not want it; and as for punishment, we cannot bear it.*

Then, in the report of al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās, Allah said to Adam (peace be upon him): "I have offered the Amānah to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, and they could not bear it. Will you take it on?" He said, "O Lord, what does it involve?" He said, "If you do good, you will be rewarded, and if you do evil, you will be punished." So Adam (peace be upon him) took the amānah and bore it — and that is the meaning of *"But man bore it."*

Tafsīr Qurṭubī, with reference to Ḥakīm Tirmidhī, reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ described this same exchange with Adam (peace be upon him), and added a sobering coda: from the moment he assumed the burden of this heavy trust, not much time had passed — not even as much as lies between the ʿAṣr and Ẓuhr prayers — before Shayṭān snared him into that well-known slip, and he was made to leave Jannah.

**When did this happen?** From Ibn ʿAbbās's report it seems the offer to the heavens, earth and mountains was made *before* the creation of Adam (peace be upon him), and was then recounted to him afterwards. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that what is apparent is that it also preceded the Covenant of Eternity, the Covenant of *Alast* — *"Am I not your Lord?"* — because that covenant is itself a phase of this very acceptance.

**And why did Adam (peace be upon him) accept?** Because, as Mazharī and Bayān ul Qurʼān explain, it had already been eternally decreed that Allah would appoint Adam (peace be upon him) His *khalīfah* (vicegerent) on the earth — and that vicegerency could only be entrusted to one who bears the responsibility of upholding the essential obedience to divine injunctions, since the very objective of this khilāfah is that the Law of Allah be implemented on earth. So Adam (peace be upon him) agreed to bear this burden, even though the inability of those other humongous units of creation was already in his knowledge.

## "Verily, he was unjust and ignorant"

Ayah 72 ends: *innahū kāna ẓalūman jahūlā.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses the two words precisely: **ẓalūm** means one who is unjust *to himself*; **jahūl** means one who is *unaware of the end* — of where a thing will finally lead. Ibn Kathir's gloss, from Ibn ʿAbbās, is of a piece with this: "he underestimated the command of Allah."

It is generally assumed that this is a blanket rebuke: how ignorant of man to take on a burden beyond his power. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that, in the light of explicit statements in the Qurʼān, this is not so.

- If "man" here means **Adam (peace be upon him)** — he is, as a prophet, protected by Allah from committing sins. The burden he assumed was carried out by him duly: he was made Allah's vicegerent and sent to the earth, he was made the object of prostration by the angels, and in the Hereafter his station is far higher than theirs.
- If "man" means **mankind as a class** — that class contains several hundred thousand noble prophets and several millions of the righteous and the friends of Allah (*awliyāʼ Allāh*) whom even angels emulate, who proved by their conduct that they were capable of deserving this divine trust. It was on the foundation laid by these very noble souls that the Qurʼān could declare: *"And We bestowed dignity on the Children of Adam"* (al-Isrāʼ 17:70).

So the sentence appears as **a description of the actual event with regard to most individuals in the class**. The majority proved *ẓalūm* and *jahūl* in failing the rights and demands of this trust and falling into the abyss of loss; and since this was the state of affairs with the majority, it was attributed to humankind. Concretely, the two words are used for those particular individuals who did not obey the injunctions of the Sharīʿah as they were expected to: the disbelievers, the hypocrites, the transgressors, the wicked, and sinning Muslims of the community. This interpretation is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others (Qurṭubī).

**A second, gentler reading.** Others have said that *ẓalūm* and *jahūl* are used here in the sense of "naive" — an affectionate form of address carrying the thought that man, brimming with love for his Creator and in quest of the station of nearness to Him, simply forgot the end of the whole thing. On this reading the words could also be taken as spoken for the entire humankind. Tafsīr Mazharī reports the details of this aspect from Mujaddid Alf Thānī and other noble Sufis.

## Ayah 73: not the purpose, but the outcome

Ayah 73 opens with the particle *li-* — "so that Allah will punish…" In common usage that *lām* mentions a cause or aim, which would sound as though the trust was given in order to produce punishment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies it instead as the **lām of ʿāqibah** — the *lām* that points out the end of something rather than its aim. The Arabic line quoted to illustrate it:

> *"Be born only to be dead, and build only to be ruined."*

It means the end of everyone born is death and the end of every building is ruin. So too here: **as a result of man's assumption of responsibility for the trust, mankind will split into two groups.**

**Group one — those who wasted it.** Disbelievers, hypocrites and others who rebel against divine orders and become wasters of the great trust. They will be punished. Ibn Kathir specifies: the **hypocrites** are those who make an outward display of faith because they fear the believers, while in their hearts they conceal disbelief and are in fact followers of the disbelievers; the **idolaters** are those who, both outwardly and inwardly, associate others in worship with Allah and go against His Messengers.

**Group two — those who kept it.** *"And Allah will pardon the believers, men and women"* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, He will show mercy to the believers among mankind, who believe in Allah and in His angels, Books and Messengers, and who obey Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this last sentence supports the reading of *ẓalūm* and *jahūl* above: those words were not meant for the whole of mankind, since ayah 73 itself distinguishes the believing men and women from those who wasted the trust.

Notice too that every category is named **in both genders** — hypocrite men and hypocrite women, idolater men and idolater women, believing men and believing women. The trust was laid on the human being as such, and so is the reckoning.

And the sūrah does not end on punishment. It ends: *"And Allah is Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

## From the Sunnah

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān bring the hadith of Ḥudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him) here. Ibn Kathir names it as recorded by Imam Aḥmad, adding that it was also recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of al-Aʿmash; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names it as in the Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim and in the *Musnad* of Aḥmad. Ḥudhayfah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told them two things: one he had already seen with his own eyes, and one whose unfolding he was still waiting to see.

The first: that **al-amānah is deeply rooted in the heart of man** — then the Qurʼān was revealed, and the people of faith came to know it from the Qurʼān and to practise it from the Sunnah.

The second, still awaited: that the amānah would be taken away. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"A man may sleep and al-amānah will be taken from his heart, leaving nothing but a trace like a blister left by a coal if you were to roll it over your leg — you will see it protruding but there is nothing inside."* Then he took a pebble and rolled it over his leg, and said: *"Then the people will start buying and selling, and hardly anyone will be paying attention to al-amānah, until it will be said that among the tribe of so-and-so there is a trustworthy man; and it will be said of a man, 'how strong he is, how nice and how wise' — and there is not even a mustard seed of faith in his heart."* Ḥudhayfah added that there had come a time when he did not mind bargaining with anyone — if the man was a Muslim, his Islam would compel him to pay what was due; and if he was a Christian or a Jew, the Muslim official would compel him — "but today, I do not deal except with such and such person among you."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson: in this hadith the amānah has been declared to be **something which relates to the heart**, and this alone has the ability of fulfilling the obligations and duties imposed by the Sharīʿah of Islam.

The second hadith both sources cite is from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr (may Allah be pleased with him), recorded by Imam Aḥmad, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"There are four things, if you attain them, then whatever you miss in this world will not matter: preserving trust, speaking the truth, being of good character and moderation in eating."* Trustworthiness heads the list.

## Living it

**Take the size of what you are carrying seriously.** Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss on *jahūl* is that man "underestimated the command of Allah." The heavens, the earth and the mountains, by contrast, drew back precisely because they weighed it. If prayer, fasting, ghusl, guarding chastity, honouring properties held under trust — the very examples the early scholars gave for *amānah* — feel like small routine items, that is exactly the miscalculation the ayah names.

**Guard the heart, because that is where the trust is kept.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's lesson from Ḥudhayfah's hadith is that amānah is a matter of the heart; and the image of the ember and the blister warns that it can be withdrawn quietly, in one night's sleep, leaving only a trace with nothing inside. Note also where the hadith locates the loss: in people entering into transactions and contracts, and no one fulfilling the trust due against him.

**Do not read the verse as despair.** Ibn Kathir closes his comment on ayah 72 with exactly the right balance: man accepted this responsibility despite the fact that he is weak, ignorant and unjust — *"except for those whom Allah helps, and Allah is the One Whose help we seek."* The trust is heavier than the heavens; the help of the One who offered it is heavier still. And ayah 73 ends with forgiveness and mercy, which is where Sūrah al-Aḥzāb is allowed to rest. And Allah, Pure and High, knows best.
